item.title: Operate Claude Managed Agents inside your security perimeter
item.content:encoded:
Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Developers can build agents that work directly in their company's code and internal systems, and run those agents in their own environment.

Self-hosting is a new way to run Managed Agents, a suite of composable APIs for building and deploying autonomous agents. Managed Agents provides the agent harness, sandboxes, credential handling, and session history to get long-running agents into production.

Run your agent control plane in your own environment

We first launched Managed Agents as a hosted service on the Claude Platform, where Anthropic runs the infrastructure for you. For teams who needed their code to stay in their own environment, we added self-hosted sandboxes.

Since then, agents have become more capable and are taking on more critical work, like fixing broken builds, testing releases, triaging alerts, and working through your bug backlog. They run unattended on your code and need access to your internal systems. For agents with that level of access, some teams want the whole service in their own environment, not just the sandbox. Until now, that meant building the platform themselves.

With self-hosted Managed Agents, every part of the service runs in your own cloud or on-premise, including the harness, sandboxes, credentials, and session history. You operate the Managed Agents server, its database, and the workers where agents run their shell and file tools. Model requests go where you choose, whether that's Anthropic directly, your cloud provider (Amazon Bedrock, Google's Agent Platform, or Microsoft Foundry), or your own gateway. Your developers still build agents with the same core APIs as the hosted Managed Agents service.

Session history is stored in your own database. If your organization has zero data retention (ZDR) in place with Anthropic, it applies to the requests sent to Claude in the same way as any other Messages API call.

Designed for agent security

When an agent runs unattended inside your code and systems, you can't rely on a person checking every step, so the limits have to be built into the system itself. That's why agent security starts with architecture, and why we designed Managed Agents around four principles. These principles apply whether Anthropic hosts everything, you host just the sandbox, or you host the whole service.

The brain and the hands are split

The harness (the brain) calls Claude, and the sandbox (the hands) is where the agent's code runs. They are kept separate by design. The agent's code runs in the sandbox, while the agent loop, session history, and vault secrets stay outside it. Separating them also means an agent doesn't depend on one sandbox surviving its whole run, sandboxes start only when a tool needs them, and session history lives outside the sandbox as an event log.

Credentials stay out of the sandbox

Vaults are designed to keep credentials out of the sandbox. For MCP tools and supported API calls, a proxy outside the sandbox adds the credential to the request. With self-hosted Managed Agents, you can also store credentials in your own secrets manager.

Network access can be limited

You can limit each environment to a list of allowed hosts, and requests to any other host are blocked. For an agent that fixes broken builds, that list might be just your git host and your package registry. When you host the sandbox yourself, you set the same limits in your own firewall.

Every session leaves a full record

Managed Agents keeps a record of every step an agent took, including the tool calls it made and what came back. The record exports over OpenTelemetry, so you can send it to the monitoring tools you already use and review agent activity alongside the rest of your systems.

Get started

Self-hosted Claude Managed Agents is now available in private beta. Contact your Anthropic account team to request access, or read the docs to learn more.

item.title: J. Crew brings its signature approach to styling to life wit…
item.description: Full title: J. Crew brings its signature approach to styling to life with Claude
item.content:encoded:
Online, shopping usually happens one product at a time, so a customer who finds a sweater has to search again for the pants and shoes that go with it. To change that, J.Crew today launched Style Advisor, an AI stylist on JCrew.com (opens in new tab) that helps customers shop by complete outfit. J.Crew’s team built it with Claude Code (opens in new tab) using multiple Claude models, from Fable to Haiku, each matched to the work it does best. It is available now for women’s and men’s styles in the U.S.

For more than 40 years, J.Crew’s own stylists have built complete looks by balancing proportion, color, and layering and by pairing pieces in unexpected ways. Style Advisor brings that expertise online. Customers describe what they need, such as an outfit for a beach wedding or a first job interview, and it answers with complete looks drawn from J.Crew’s own photo shoots. They can keep refining from there, so shopping becomes a visual conversation.

How it's built

J.Crew’s product team used Claude Fable (opens in new tab) 5.1, Anthropic’s model for complex, open-ended work, to plan how Style Advisor should reason like a stylist, then built a working prototype with Claude Opus (opens in new tab) 5.5 in Claude Code. J.Crew’s engineers took that prototype to production. In each conversation, Claude Sonnet (opens in new tab) 5.5 acts as the stylist and decides each step of the response, while Claude Haiku (opens in new tab) 5.5 handles quick, focused tasks so Style Advisor answers quickly. Because every look comes from J.Crew’s stylists, its recommendations stay consistent with J.Crew’s styling point of view.

How customers use Style Advisor

  • Shop complete outfits. Every recommendation starts from looks J.Crew stylists created for the brand's catalog shoots, and Style Advisor shows them in photos so customers see the full outfit.
  • Build from a single piece. A customer can start with one item and get suggestions for the pieces that complete the look.
  • Dress for the occasion. Customers can say where they're going, whether that's a vacation, a holiday party, or a wedding, and get recommendations for it.
  • Get J.Crew's point of view. Style Advisor applies the same styling principles a J.Crew stylist would use in a store.

What's next

At launch, Style Advisor helps customers find new outfit ideas and shop with more confidence. Over time, J.Crew plans to make it more personal by tailoring suggestions to each customer's preferences and past purchases, and to bring it to more markets and product lines.

“As consumer expectations evolve and AI opens up new possibilities for retail, J.Crew is challenging the traditional model of online shopping, moving beyond individual product searches toward a more connected and inspiration-led experience,” said Libby Wadle, Chief Executive Officer of J.Crew Group. “For a long time, we’ve been thinking about how customers will want to shop in the future, and how we can lead that evolution rather than react to it. We see an opportunity to fundamentally rethink the shopping experience. Through our work with Anthropic, we're bringing decades of J.Crew styling, merchandising and creative expertise together to help shape what’s next for customer behavior.”

“J.Crew has one of the most recognizable points of view in fashion, and its team used Claude to bring that expertise to customers in a new way,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic. “They used a frontier model to build the experience and faster, more efficient models to run it, so customers get quick answers that stay true to the brand’s styling.”

Start building with Claude Code (opens in new tab) today.

item.title: Introducing Claude for Manufacturing
item.content:encoded:
Today we’re launching Claude for Manufacturing (opens in new tab), a plugin that includes skills for work from pricing a new job to diagnosing a stopped machine. An estimator can now have Claude read a customer’s request, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote. The plugin works from a manufacturer’s own records through connectors to Autodesk Fusion, Infor, Microsoft 365, and Oracle NetSuite. Claude for Manufacturing is built so the person responsible can review and approve the work before it reaches a customer or supplier.

Manufacturing teams can spend much of the day gathering information. In a 2025 Manufacturing Leadership Council survey, 79% of manufacturers said they enter data (opens in new tab)manually. With Claude carrying each process to the point of review, an estimator can focus on the price, a quality engineer on the fix, and a technician on what to check first.

Skills built for manufacturers

The plugin’s 17 skills cover sales, quality, operations, supply chain, design, and setup. Some handle a single task, while others run several in order, so Claude can carry a job through several steps until a person needs to review it. The skills can run processes that include:

  • Quoting a new job: An estimator can ask Claude to read a customer’s request, list what’s missing, compare costs on similar jobs, and draft the quote for release.
  • Investigating a failed inspection: A quality engineer can have Claude document the failure, check past reports for the same problem, rank the likely causes, and draft the corrective action report.
  • Diagnosing a breakdown: A technician can have Claude read the sensor exports, repair notes, photos, and manual, then rank the likely causes for the technician to check and decide on next steps.
  • Sourcing from another supplier: A buyer can have Claude prepare the request for quotes, then compare the bids that come back.
  • Comparing designs with Autodesk Fusion: An engineer can have Claude generate variations from an existing model, score them against the engineer’s targets, and draft a decision memo.
  • Reporting on production: A plant manager can have Claude compile production data into one report showing output against target, equipment downtime, and what the downtime and missed output cost.

These skills are a starting point. Organizations can build on them to fit their specific operations, and we plan to add new manufacturing skills over time.

Connectors to manufacturing systems

Claude for Manufacturing works with the software at the core of manufacturing operations, and that software stays central to how teams run the business:

  • Autodesk Fusion: Engineers can compare more design options before choosing one, because Claude generates variations from their existing model.
  • Infor: Buyers and planners can check purchase orders and stock before they act, because Claude looks them up in Infor.
  • Microsoft 365: Quality engineers can bring procedures, supplier emails, and exported reports into one job, because Claude finds them in shared folders and inboxes.
  • Oracle NetSuite: Estimators can price new work against actual orders, inventory, production steps, and job costs, because Claude pulls those records when it drafts a quote.

Manufacturers can also use the plugin with systems that have no connector. They save regular exports from those systems to Microsoft 365, and Claude works from the files to draft a quote or compile a production report.

Making changes in Infor with Claude

Infor, which makes core software for manufacturers, is also releasing its own plugin (opens in new tab). With the Infor connector in Claude for Manufacturing, teams can look up records. With Infor’s plugin, they can also make changes in Infor from Claude.

For example, if a steel shipment slips by two weeks, a buyer can ask Claude which customer orders are affected and how much steel other sites have. Once the buyer approves, Claude can release a purchase order to another supplier and reschedule the affected production in Infor. Claude’s access follows the buyer’s Infor permissions.

Manufacturing teams stay in control

Skills are built to end with a user’s review, so an estimator checks and releases a quote, and a quality engineer verifies a fix for the corrective action report. To support that review, Claude can link figures and claims back to the underlying data and documents.

Claude for Manufacturing doesn’t operate equipment. For that, Anthropic is developing the Model Hardware Standard (opens in new tab), a research preview that gives programmable equipment a standard way to describe its measurements, settings, and safety limits.

How to get started

On Team or Enterprise plans, install the plugin (opens in new tab) and tell Claude, “Set us up.” Claude asks which systems the team uses, tests the connectors, and reports which skills can’t fully run yet.

To see the plugin at work, register for our technical webinar (opens in new tab) on November 17 at 11:00 a.m. ET. To talk through a company’s manufacturing systems, contact our sales team (opens in new tab).

item.title: Introducing Claude Meetings
item.content:encoded:
Claude can now join your video calls as a visible participant, follow the conversation and start on work during the meeting. Claude Meetings is now in beta.

Your team can ask Claude questions during the meeting, out loud or in chat. By default, Claude answers in writing, and it can use your connected tools with your permission.

Claude also works with you live to build docs, whiteboards (opens in new tab), or other artifacts, while teammates on the invite refine them. Claude writes the notes and action items, so no one on the call has to.

Claude Meetings is starting to roll out in beta on Team and Enterprise plans. Support for other video conferencing platforms is coming soon.

What it looks like

Say your team is planning a customer event, and Claude is on the call. You say, “Claude, start a doc for this plan.” Claude writes up what the team has said so far, and teammates on the invite can edit the plan while you keep talking.

When you start discussing the budget, someone asks Claude what last year’s event cost. Claude asks for their approval to look it up, posts it in the meeting chat, and compares it to the current plan. When you start discussing timelines, someone asks Claude to put it on a whiteboard, and the team works on the schedule alongside the doc.

Before the meeting ends, someone asks Claude to share a recap with the team. After the call, any notes, action items, plan, and whiteboard are on the meeting’s page in claude.ai (opens in new tab).

Later, you can go back to meetings you were part of and ask Claude about them, or add Claude to the next one from your calendar in claude.ai.

We’re working with partners like Gong, Attention, Granola, Fireflies.ai, Otter, and Plaud, so you’ll soon be able to send a meeting’s transcript to the tools your team already uses.

Security and privacy

Claude adds a separate page for each meeting in claude.ai (opens in new tab) with the notes, transcript, and anything it built. People from your organization on the invite can see it and edit what Claude made, and it can be shared with others in your organization from the page.

By default, Claude is set to stay out of calls when someone from outside your organization is invited, and to leave if someone from outside joins partway through. An admin can allow Claude on calls with outside guests. On those calls, Claude posts its notice in the call’s chat but doesn’t reply there, and what guests say is included in the notes and transcript.

Claude uses each person’s connected tools with that person’s permission. It asks the first time, and a yes applies going forward. For now, when someone asks out loud, Claude asks each time to confirm who’s speaking. An answer posted in the call’s chat is visible to everyone on the call.

When Claude joins, it appears as a participant and posts a notice in the call’s chat. It saves a transcript, summary, and screen descriptions, not audio.

Before you add Claude or turn on auto-join, make sure everyone on your calls is OK with being transcribed.

Getting started

Claude joins when someone adds it or has auto-join on. Support is currently available for Google Meet, with other platforms coming soon. On Team plans, inviting Claude to your meetings is available by default, and an admin can turn it off. On Enterprise plans, an admin turns it on for all or part of the organization. While it’s in beta, it isn’t available to some organizations, including those with zero data retention (ZDR), HIPAA-ready configuration, or customer-managed encryption keys (CMEK).

During the beta, Claude’s notes and transcripts are free on Team and Enterprise plans. So are its answers in your calls, unless an answer uses one of your connected tools, which counts toward your plan’s usage. The docs, whiteboards, (opens in new tab) and other artifacts Claude makes in a call are free through February 10, 2027.

Setup steps are in the Help Center.

item.title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge wor…
item.description: Full title: Using Claude Opus 5.5 as your daily driver for knowledge work
item.content:encoded:
Claude Opus 5.5 is now the default model in Claude on Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans. We recommend it as your daily driver for knowledge work, meaning the model you leave selected when you work with Claude on research, analysis, and writing or producing memos, reports, spreadsheets, and decks.

If you or your team have been using Sonnet for daily work and saving Opus for heavy analysis or complex projects, it’s worth reconsidering because a more capable model can finish a task by doing less work, which can then offset much of its higher price per token.

Here's how the current models compare:

ModelUse it forPrice per million tokens (input / output)*Relative speed
Claude Haiku 5.5Quick lookups and high-volume work where speed matters most$0.10 / $0.50Fastest
Claude Sonnet 5.5Quick, well-scoped tasks, and polished documents, slides, and spreadsheets from a clear brief$2 / $10Fast
Claude Opus 5.5Most knowledge work: research, analysis, and finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets that need judgment$4 / $20Moderate
Claude Fable 5.2The most ambitious, open-ended technical work, in fields like coding, finance, and the sciences$8 / $40Moderate

**Prices are for usage billed by the token (model comparison). Haiku 5.5's prices apply to prompts up to 100k tokens, and longer prompts cost $0.50 / $2.50. On Pro, Max, Ultra, and Team plans, higher-priced models use your limits faster. Pro plans and standard seats on Team and seat-based Enterprise plans don’t include Fable 5.2 in their limits outside limited-time launch offers, so it runs on usage credits.*

Haiku 5.5 is our fastest and least expensive model, built for quick lookups and high-volume work like writing summaries and sorting data. This is our first Haiku model with effort controls, so you can ask for a more careful pass before switching to a larger model. It’s best suited to short, narrowly scoped tasks. For longer analysis, switch to Opus 5.5.

Sonnet 5.5 is faster and cheaper than Opus 5.5 for well-scoped tasks that have a clear brief. This could be asking Claude to turn finished notes into a polished document, or to build a deck using a slide template. At higher-effort settings, however, cost per task with Sonnet 5.5 gets close to Opus 5.5, so if you find yourself pushing Sonnet to Extra high or Max effort, consider switching to Opus 5.5.

Opus 5.5 is built for complex work that needs careful judgment, like research, financial analysis, and producing finished docs, decks, and spreadsheets. We share details on why we recommend Opus 5.5 for daily knowledge work later.

Fable 5.2 is best for your most demanding reasoning and long-running work, like deep multi-step research or coding that you can hand off to a large team of subagents that run for hours. For most knowledge work, start with Opus 5.5 and move to Fable 5.2 when a project’s scope and complexity calls for it. Fable 5.2 is available on all paid plans, though how it draws on your usage depends on your plan.

Whichever model you're on, if Claude didn’t do as well as you expected, try a higher effort first before moving up a model. If it had the context, clearly tried, and still got it wrong, move up a model.

Opus 5.5 does its best work on documents, research, finance, and charts

Opus 5.5 follows instructions precisely and stays in scope, so the spreadsheets, slides, and documents it produces often need little editing. It's careful with figures and sources, too. In one internal research test, Opus 5.5 wrote reports on a company's quarterly performance using only a saved snapshot of the web, in which the company’s earnings release was hard to locate. An automated grader checked every figure and quote against the pages in that snapshot, under a condition that the report would fail if even a single figure or quote was invented. Across effort settings, 16 of its 18 reports passed.

Its writing is clearer than that of earlier models, too. Opus 5.5 puts the most important information first, uses less jargon, and follows the writing rules you give it, and on longer tasks it says plainly what it did, what it found, and what it needs from you. That also makes its work easier to check, which we count as a safety benefit as well as a practical one.

John Ruelas, a staff software engineer at Ramp, said: “It writes like a good colleague, and follows our writing rules. A design spec came out usable with very minimal edits, and when it rewrote one of our prompts I preferred its version to my own.”

Financial analysis is another strength. Opus 5.5 reads dense filings, financial models, and charts accurately and keeps track of context across a whole project or deal. In another internal test, it analyzed a proposed merger between two fictional HR software companies, building a financial model in Excel and then turning it into an executive presentation on whether the deal made sense at its price. It finished in 63 minutes, compared with 93 for Opus 5 on the same task, at half the cost, with a more thorough model, and an easier-to-read presentation.

Frank Corrao, who leads central equity quant research engineering at investment firm Walleye Capital, said that at higher effort settings, Opus 5.5 “detected that the minute indexing in our own instructions was off by one and corrected for it, noting that this would cost it points with the grader. It was right, and no model we’ve tested had caught and acted on that before.”

Opus 5.5 is our best Opus model for vision. It reads dense documents, charts, screenshots, and diagrams accurately, which makes it reliable for pulling data out of documents. Even at its lowest effort setting, it read values off dense charts more accurately than Opus 5 did at its highest.

Getting more out of Opus 5.5

Each new model is a reason to retest what you hand to Claude and to drop prompting habits built for older models.

Try these tasks first

  • Ask for a finished file. If you want a spreadsheet or a document, ask for the spreadsheet or document rather than an outline to build from. More often than not, Opus 5.5 can get from your request to the finished file in one pass.
  • Have it check long documents. Give it a long plan, report, or deck and ask it to find mistakes and inconsistencies. Opus 5.5 catches details that are easy to miss in long documents, such as a chart in a deck that doesn’t match its source data.
  • Hand it a research question. Ask a question without a set answer and have it pull sources together, work through long documents, and write up what it finds as a memo, report, or deck.
  • Try visual work. Its vision gains carry over to design, so try it for prototyping an interface, building a website, or illustrating a concept.

Change these prompting habits

  • Connect Claude to your work files and systems. This is one of the most useful steps for getting output that fits your work, because when Claude can reach your files and systems through connectors, it can go get what a task needs instead of working only from what you paste in. On Team and Enterprise plans, an owner has to turn a connector on before members can use it.
  • Say what done looks like in your first message. Instead of prompting Claude with instructions one at a time, describe your goal, the finished output, and when you want it to stop and ask. Opus 5.5 carries long, multipart work through to the end better than Opus 5 did.
  • Delete “think hard” and “think carefully.” Thinking is always on for Opus 5.5, and it decides how much to think based on your request and the effort level. In our testing, removing those lines made replies start sooner, with no clear drop in quality.
  • Start at Medium effort. Medium is the default for Opus 5.5, and on our coding and knowledge-work evaluations, Opus 5.5 at Medium matched or beat Opus 5 at High. Higher settings think longer and cost more without always producing better work, so move up to High when Medium stalls. To change the setting, click the model name next to the send button and choose Effort.
  • Attach the chart instead of retyping it. Share the chart, screenshot, or diagram itself rather than copying its numbers into the prompt. Workarounds built for earlier models, like transcribing a chart's values, may no longer be needed.
  • Name the styles you don't want. For design work, a general instruction like “avoid a generic look” tends to swap one default style for another. Naming specific patterns to avoid, such as a cream background or pill-shaped buttons, works better.
  • Give it your house style. Paste your brand or writing guidelines into the request, or point Claude to your best existing decks, for example in a Google Drive folder it can reach through a connector, and ask it to match them. Expect a few rounds before it's exactly right.

The effort finding held for early testers, too. Zimu Li, Member of Technical Staff at Factory, said, “Claude Opus 5.5 is the first model we’d default to at medium effort. In our testing it matched Opus 5 on high effort, while using 20 to 25% fewer output tokens.”

Testing Opus 5.5 on a demo project

Here's what all this looks like on one project we worked through in a demo. At a hypothetical retail company, revenue growth had slowed over the past year, leadership had four theories about why, and an analyst had a folder of material: spreadsheets of sales by store, PDFs from the latest leadership off-site, and other files. With Opus 5.5 at Medium effort, the prompt read, roughly:

Growth slowed a lot this year. Leadership has a couple of theories about why; they're in [my manager's] note. Everything I have is in the uploaded folder. Please test each of the four theories against the data and tell me which ones hold up.

The prompt doesn't tell Claude to think hard, and it doesn't say which file to check for which theory. It states the goal and what the final output looks like, and leaves the approach to Claude.

Claude found that the data didn't support any of the four theories, though one couldn't be fully ruled out. It then proposed an explanation that nobody had raised: new stores had opened too close to existing ones and were drawing sales away from them. The pattern was a little unclear with the stores listed by city, and clear once they were filtered by proximity to a new store. Claude backed the finding with a regression of the sales impact against that distance.

Next, Claude turned the analysis into a document that holds charts and interactive elements alongside text, including a slider showing how sales change with the distance between a new store and an existing one. A teammate reviewed the doc at the same time.

The manager then asked Claude to turn the doc into board slides that opened with the answer. For teammates who don't use Claude, docs export to Word, PDF, or Google Docs, and decks export to PowerPoint, PDF, or Google Slides.

To see the whole project, including the Q&A, watch the Opus 5.5 for Work session on demand.

Try Opus 5.5 on your own work

Pick something you'd normally split across several requests, like a research memo, a variance analysis, or a deck built from an existing doc. Give Opus 5.5 the files and a description of the finished result in one message, leave it at Medium effort, and compare the result with what you're used to getting from other models.

item.title: The Claude Tag guide for startups
item.content:encoded:
Startups frequently work at a fast pace with lean teams wearing many hats. In many ways, Claude Tag (beta) is suited for how startups work. You @Claude to a Slack channel where your context lives, add connectors, and have your team assign and steer tasks together.

For startup teams new to using Claude Tag, one of the most frequent questions is “which channels should I add Claude to first?” To help answer it, we spoke with eight high growth startups to see how Claude Tag works inside their teams.

Featuring insights from

We heard from leaders at companies with visions from reinventing law firms to building the next generation of resource planning software. Some had added Claude to nearly every channel while others had focused deeply on one or two specific use cases.

CompanyOn callThread to PRCompany brainSelf-serve dataRoutine reporting
Kikoff●●●●
NavigateAI●●●●
Campfire●●●
Flagler Health●●●
Moritz●●
Orderful●●●●
Valence●●●
Descript●●●

But everyone we spoke with shared an “aha!” moment where they realized a minutes-long Claude Tag conversation replaced days of work or uncovered insights that would otherwise have remained hidden.

The most common are contained in this guide, each with practical implementation details designed to help founders find and deploy the use cases that will move the needle for their team. Here are some examples of how the needle moved for the startups we spoke with:

21

minutes from Slack mention to open PR

134

pull requests merged from Slack threads

5

minutes for the daily end-of-shift update, down from 1 hour

<1

hour from client ask to no-code solution

2

days from Slack question to production

Days to hours

of recurring reporting prep

In this guide, we share the most common use cases, channels, and collective insights from leading startups for using Claude Tag.

Top channels to tag Claude

The eight startups we spoke with use Claude Tag across Slack, but a handful of channels came up again and again as the best places to start.

01 Claude on call

Example setups:

Channels

#on-call #alerts-ci #deploy-watch #support-escalations

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Sentry, dbt, PagerDuty, Linear, Datadog, Jira, Grafana, incident.io

Threads and routines

Incident response, morning incident digest, Monday on-call handoff, daily health summary, hourly incident recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: monitor alerts and immediately triage each one in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket. Query the data first, then theorize, and separate what you verified from what you inferred. If it's real, name the likely root cause with links, tag the owner, and open a draft PR only if the fix is contained. If no action is needed, say so. After each incident, add what you learned to [lessons file].

Triage channels are notoriously noisy. There are constant interruptions from Sentry errors, Datadog alerts, customer bug reports, and support requests making it difficult to find the signal from noise. It's usually the first task teams hand to Claude.

With Claude in the channel as a first responder, the first pass is often done before the on-call engineer opens their laptop. Claude reads each item as it lands, investigates the codebase and the tools it has access to, and shares what it found. If the fix is contained, it opens a draft PR; if not, it routes the issue to the right person with the investigation attached. In these setups, a person reviews each fix before it merges, and only genuinely new problems need someone to start the investigation themselves.

At Campfire, which builds an AI-native ERP for finance teams, an engineer tagged Claude on a report that some of its AI agent’s finished answers weren’t reaching users. Claude had a PR open 21 minutes later, and it merged that afternoon.

Kikoff: A first responder in every triage channel

Kikoff is a fintech startup that helps consumers build credit, solve liquidity needs, and achieve financial security. Claude Tag is the first responder in triage channels across the company, including:

  • #deploys: Claude decides what to watch after each release and flags anything it broke.
  • #alerts-ci: When a build fails, Claude finds out why and proposes a fix as a draft PR.
  • #alerts-sentry-backend: Claude takes the first pass on Sentry exceptions and crashes.
  • #dog-fooding: Claude investigates what employees flag while dogfooding and tags the right owner.
  • #support: Claude takes the first pass on support tickets.

Kikoff started with Claude contributing to the conversation only when mentioned, and the biggest wins came once the team let it jump in on its own. When sign-up broke, Claude traced it to a backend change, sized the impact, named the team that owned the fix, and opened a draft PR so the app would fail softly in the meantime.

Claude flags that sign-up is broken, traces it to a backend change, sizes the impact, names the team that owns the fix, and opens a draft PR so the app fails softly. A recreated conversation from Kikoff. Names and images have been modified. Used with permission from Kikoff.

“I’m always hyped when Claude catches an issue before a monitor or human does. One person can only personally manage so much context, Claude Tag helps us organize and own some context, and we manage the outcomes.”

Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff

NavigateAI: Fixing bugs with fragmented context

NavigateAI builds AI copilots for construction field teams. They run Claude Tag in about 90 channels for alert triage, bug bashes, quick feature building, and support escalations. Since June, Claude has opened about 223 PRs straight from Slack threads and 134 have merged with a median of two hours from open to merge.

Triage has been a particularly valuable use case for NavigateAI. Because Claude has so much context, it can find unintuitive root causes to issues that may have been missed at first glance.

“Our biggest ‘wow!’ moment with Claude Tag was when we were trying to debug a load issue, which seemed to be caused by a customer (since their calls were failing). A normal human response would be to continue chasing down that customer. But because Claude had access to so many other data sources, it actually found that it was from an uninstrumented internal cron job that was running during the same time.”

Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI

With Claude, mean time to resolve issues has improved. In one case, Claude had the root cause eight minutes after a Sentry alert fired, and the fix was merged 93 minutes after the alert.

“Fast-moving startups typically have to pick speed over structure. Claude Tag gives us both. It’s a brain that connects the dots across all our tools, so we get the structure without having to build it ourselves,” said Mike.

02 Thread to PR

Example setups:

Channels

#quick-wins #bug-bash #product-feedback #feature-requests #ux-papercuts #tech-debt #design-polish

Connectors

GitHub, GitLab, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Notion, Figma, Sentry

Threads and routines

One request per thread, weekly backlog sweep, daily PR roundup, weekly shipped recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: when someone describes a bug or small feature, work on it in its own thread. Check for an existing ticket and read the related code first. If details are missing, ask for them or for a real example instead of guessing. If the change is small and contained, open a draft PR with a short summary of what changed and how you tested it. Never merge; a person reviews and approves. If it's too big or risky, say why and suggest a ticket.

Speed is one of a startup’s biggest advantages, but often small requests that delight users can get lost in the shuffle. The intelligence is often gathered by customer-facing teams, submitted in Slack, and, if it's not overlooked, eventually makes its way to Linear or Jira where it’s prioritized against hundreds of other tickets.

With Claude Tag, anyone can draft the PR, technical or not. Surface an idea in a thread, get live feedback from product, engineering, and GTM in the same place, and Claude turns the thread into a draft PR that reflects everyone’s input.

Many of the startups we spoke with used Claude Tag for the “light and delight” features or to remove papercuts that are quick to review but would otherwise not get prioritized.

Orderful: From Slack exchange to production feature in two days

Orderful is an EDI platform that connects companies with their trading partners, through an API or straight from the browser. Its customers trade standard documents with their partners through the platform.

One document type, the 753, wasn’t supported in Orderful’s web app. The request had sat in the backlog, and shipments for one large retailer were delayed.

When an account manager followed up in Slack, the PM tagged Claude in: “@Claude, you should build one.” Claude asked for real examples of the document so it could build to the actual format, then opened a draft PR adding 753 support.

Claude confirms a fix works on a real 753 transaction. Names and images have been changed. Used with permission from Orderful.

The next morning, Claude filed a ticket for the accompanying 754, the retailer’s response, and opened a second PR. Both were in production about two days after the Slack exchange.

“Something that took weeks or months before just took a Slack conversation,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful. “Light features with hard-to-prove value used to get stuck in the backlog. Now they have a way out.”

Valence: From feature request to rollout

Valence works with the world’s largest employers to connect enterprise talent and performance with Nadia, an AI coach. When a Valence engineer explained in Slack how to address an urgent product change requested by an important client, Claude didn’t just follow directions, it identified additional changes that needed to be made as the same configuration lived in two spots. Without Claude, the initial change would have been incomplete.

Claude calls out that a requested change is actually two changes. Used with permission from Valence.

“It didn’t just agree with the expert. It caught duplicated configuration, the kind of thing humans lose track of.”

Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence

In another case, a client urgently asked for a customization. Claude checked the code and, working with an engineer, confirmed it could ship with no code change. In under an hour, a teammate had a solution ready for the client.

03 Company brain

Example setups:

Channels

#ask-anything #company-wiki #product-questions

Connectors

GitHub, Notion, Google Drive, Linear, Jira, Confluence, Granola, Metabase

Threads and routines

One question per thread, decision log updates, weekly stale doc check, repeat questions recap

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer questions from our code, docs and past threads, and link your sources. If sources disagree, check the code, give the current answer, and flag the stale doc. If you aren’t sure, say so and tag the owner. When a thread reaches a decision, record it in [docs location]. Anything going to a client needs a human check first.

At a startup, institutional knowledge often lives in people's heads, from the intricacies of product billing codes to where the onboarding docs are hosted.

For many of the startups we spoke with, Claude Tag has become the company brain. Claude answers with the source, and tags the owner when it isn't confident. It keeps that knowledge current too: when a thread reaches a decision, Claude can record it in your docs the same day and flag docs that have gone stale.

Example exchange.

Moritz: A live source of truth from intake to staffing

Moritz is an AI-native law firm that promises a same-day turnaround on contracts, against what Moritz cites as an industry standard of at least three weeks. Everything around the legal work, from intake and quoting to staffing and follow-up, lives in Slack, with a thread per matter and a channel per client.

Now everyone from the CEO to paralegals asks Claude first. Questions that took up to 30 minutes of searching in Slack get answered in under two. The end-of-shift update, now drafted from the day’s threads, went from about an hour of assembly to a five-minute edit.

That time goes back to legal work. Claude Tag handles the administrative work around a case, like follow-up questions, reminders, and status updates. It can’t access client documents or privileged conversations with Moritz’s lawyers.

“A firm working across 44 countries generates hundreds of one-off questions a month that no one will ever build a feature for. Claude Tag answers them from our own history in Slack. Every answer is a thread with links, so institutional memory compounds.”

Stefan Mandaric, co-founder and CTO at Moritz

Campfire: Customer experience on demand

One Slack channel in particular “exploded in popularity”: their CX (or customer experience) channel. Sales uses this channel “to validate certain functionality during prospect conversations,” rather than having to “ping 10 different people.”

This type of channel is particularly effective because sales can answer in the moment, while the customer is paying attention, and can operate more independently and confidently in early customer conversations.

“Claude Tag basically acts as our central knowledge base.”

Nancy Jin, AI engineering manager at Campfire

04 Self-serve data

Example setups:

Channels

#data-requests #ask-revops #metric-definitions

Connectors

dbt, GitHub, Metabase, BigQuery, Snowflake, Databricks, Notion

Threads and routines

One question per thread, weekly pre-standup readout, launch and experiment readouts, pipeline failure triage, new question triage

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: answer from our governed models and the definitions in [data skills repo]. If the data isn’t covered there, say it’s unvalidated instead of guessing. Lead with the answer, then give the number, what’s driving it, and any caveat. Check recent incidents, releases, and Slack discussions before explaining a change. If a metric’s definition is unclear, ask which one we mean. For anything important, share your plan or SQL before you run it. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and list any open data quality warnings at the end of your answer. If someone finds a mistake, draft a fix for a data team member to review. If a question comes up twice, suggest scheduling it.

At a fast-growing startup every function wants numbers, and the data team has to decide whose request comes first. With Claude Tag connected to your data, anyone can ask in plain English without waiting in the data team’s queue.

This is a use case we have adopted as well. In one of our data channels over a month, Claude Tag answered more than 75% of questions people posted, typically within a minute or two. It works from governed data and the same definitions analysts use, which live in a versioned repo that Claude re-reads in every conversation.

From Self-service data analytics in Slack: how Anthropic deploys Claude Tag for ad-hoc questions.

Descript: Answering ad-hoc data requests

Descript is an AI-powered video editing platform. Claude Tag is now the first line of support for data requests and initial analyses. Product, growth, RevOps, and finance ask questions in Slack and get answers grounded in Descript’s dbt models.

“I used to write complicated SQL and refresh the numbers by hand every week or month. Now I’ve replaced several data-team dashboards with my own Claude artifacts, and I no longer refresh them by hand.”

Daisy Zhang, head of growth marketing at Descript

Daisy’s recurring reporting prep went from days to hours.

The growth team, for example, asks why lifecycle subscriptions dropped, whether paid search is losing last-touch credit to other channels, or how long a self-serve account takes to become an enterprise opportunity. The data team tracks the artifacts Claude generates to see which data assets matter most across teams, and spends its own time on strategic questions and on building the context that makes self-serve work.

“The promise of business intelligence has always been self-serve for business users. I’d never seen it actually realized until we had Claude Tag set up with immense context for our data.”

Jen Huhn, monetization PM at Descript

Orderful: From question to dashboard

At Orderful, self-serve analytics spans conversational analytics and full data builds: anyone can go from a question in Slack to a dashboard merged to production. The key is a semantic layer that encodes agreed definitions and metrics, so every answer and every build uses the same definitions.

“We trust the output because a semantic layer constrains the SQL, CI gates the builds, and there’s a process for agreeing on definitions. Without those, you get confident-looking wrong answers. Once those guardrails were in place, connecting Claude Tag took under 30 minutes. Now teammates build together in shared Slack threads instead of solo sessions.”

Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful

05 Reporting and handoffs

Example setups:

Channels

#sales-pipeline #customer-handoffs #standup-summary #qbr-prep

Connectors

Notion, Google Drive, Gong, Salesforce, Gainsight

Threads and routines

End-of-day status draft, pre-QBR brief, deal handoff

Starter instruction

@Claude remember for this channel: draft each recurring report from our threads, docs, and data, and link your sources. Lead with what changed and what needs a decision. Separate what you verified from what you assumed, and flag anything missing instead of filling the gap. Post the draft in its own thread for [owner] to edit. Nothing goes out until a person approves it. If a report keeps getting the same edits, suggest updating these instructions.

Many of the examples we’ve covered are reactive: something happens, Claude responds. Routine reporting is work Claude owns on a schedule, the way a teammate owns a recurring deliverable.

Example of using Routines in Claude Tag.

You describe the outcome once; Claude runs it every time and posts the result where the team already works.

Valence: Deal reviews and handoffs

Valence is setting Claude up to brief the team before every quarterly business review, with customer health, open deals, blockers, and next steps. They are also working to make the handoff from sales to customer success when a deal closes more seamless. Claude saves the team time by helping to aggregate details across their engagement and often finds key items they may have missed.

“When a deal closes, Tag builds the handoff from the deal history, calls and contract: who’s who, what was promised, what’s customized, and what’s still open. Customer success then reviews it before their kickoff,” said Sameer.

06 Getting started checklist

The checklist below pulls together these startup teams’ best practices so you can apply them to your own workflows.

Before launch

Check the prerequisites.

Claude Tag is in public beta on Claude Team and Enterprise plans, and isn’t available on Free, Pro, or Max. You’ll need a Claude organization Owner and a Slack workspace admin to connect the two. An admin must also turn on Routines, and Team plans need usage credits before Claude responds.

Set up Claude’s access with a bundle.

In channels, Claude works under its own agent identity, with service accounts rather than anyone’s personal login. Group the connectors, repos, and instructions it needs in a bundle, and attach them org-wide, per workspace, or per channel. That sets what Claude can reach in each place, and everyone in a channel gets the same access. Start narrow: only what the first channel’s job needs.

Experiment in a private channel.

Nearly half the startups we spoke with started their Claude Tag journey by having a small cross-functional team experiment in a private channel. “Start private with a mix of roles, then move to a group channel,” said Sameer.

Determine the boundaries.

By default, anyone in your Slack workspace can use Claude, even without a Claude account. You can restrict access to your org and limit search to channels Claude is in. On Enterprise, you can also restrict access to specific roles or chosen channels.

Set clear expectations for what Claude can do and can never do. Several teams we spoke with let Claude open draft PRs, but people review and merge. For Orderful, Claude Code, not Tag, handles “infrastructure changes, audits, sensitive data.” For a “hard call,” such as “a PR that touches more than one service,” Claude gets a second opinion. Moritz doesn’t give Claude Tag access to client documents or privileged conversations with its lawyers.

Start your security review early.

The usual questions are data retention and what Claude can reach, and the security and data lifecycle pages answer both. Claude Tag isn’t available to orgs with zero data retention turned on, a customer-managed encryption (CMEK) policy, or the HIPAA configuration, and it isn’t covered by our Business Associate Agreement, so check that before you plan a rollout.

Set a budget and alerts.

Claude Tag bills by usage, so an early conversation avoids surprises as adoption grows. You can set spend limits overall and per channel, choose the model per channel, and attribute costs by user using the Enterprise Analytics API. Orderful runs an org-wide cap with alerts at 75% and 90%. “We have extreme ownership on the channel costs. The owner justifies that ‘yes, this spend is reasonable for the output / outcomes,’” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff. Use your first channel’s actual costs to size the next one.

Deployment

Pick one clear task in a channel your team already uses, like on-call alerts or bug triage.

“We experiment on certain teams, see what works, then once confident we’ve worked out the kinks, we push the idea out to other teams to add to their own similar channels as well. We want to avoid trust breaking experiences with folks with lower tolerance to AI mistakes,” said Alex Dejeu, engineering manager at Kikoff.

Prime your experts and culture bearers.

Have the people your team already trusts use Claude first, and in the open.

“Going back and forth with Claude in the open has been productive and fun. Several people in sales and customer success have watched experts [interact with Claude Tag], then started asking Claude themselves, and got value fast,” said Sameer Bansal, principal AI engineer at Valence.

Tune the noise.

Multiple startups told us they needed to adjust Claude’s chattiness. Too chatty is one risk.

“Conversation in ad hoc requests can sometimes get noisy. We’ve been trying to tune down the responsiveness here and also be more principled on what we use Claude on ad hoc requests for,” said Mike Chen, head of engineering at NavigateAI.

Too little chattiness is also a risk, however. In busy channels, “You either have to @ every time or it won’t do much,” said Will Hu, cofounder at Flagler Health. And “if no one is watching a channel closely or interacts with it, it will sit idle.”

Have teammates connect their own accounts.

The admin bundles from setup are what Claude can reach for everyone in a channel. Personal connectors work differently: Claude acts with the permissions of the person asking, so it can pull from their docs, inbox, or CRM once they approve it (an Owner adds the connector for the org first, and on Enterprise an admin manages personal connectors). The answer still posts in the channel, so choose “Allow with review” for anything sensitive.

Write channel instructions like you’re onboarding a new hire:

what to check first, when to open a PR, when to ask, and that “no action needed” is a valid answer.

Give Claude feedback in the channel, not in DMs.

Correct it in the thread. It remembers per channel, and teammates learn how to work with it by watching. For a lasting fix, ask Claude to update its memory for this channel.

Two Valence employees thank a colleague after watching them work through a question with Claude in the open. Used with permission from Valence.

Not sure where to go next? Tag Claude and ask what it has learned about your org and which use cases it would expand to.

Moritz’s co-founder and CTO, Stefan Mandaric, asked Claude to recommend use cases for each team. Fifteen minutes later, it had read the firm’s Slack channels, Linear issues, Notion SOPs, Drive, and Metabase dashboards, and published 25. “18 of 25 worked with no further setup. That became our rollout plan.”

Last word: what we learned from the wow moments

The wow moments weren’t always about speed. Often, Claude found something no one had asked it to look for. Sometimes the surprise was restraint. And sometimes the surprise was the unexpected exchanges. “Eventually you get used to Claude jumping in on jokes, and you soon appreciate that it’s an easy audience and the first one to laugh,” said Piers MacDonald, CTO at Orderful.

Recreated Orderful conversation in Slack. Used with permission from Orderful.

We hope you found this guide useful. Special thanks to Campfire, Descript, Flagler Health, Kikoff, Moritz, NavigateAI, Orderful and Valence for sharing their experiences and insights.

item.title: Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in the…
item.description: Full title: Your apps can now open in Claude, and Claude can work in them
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, we launched interactive connectors (opens in new tab) to bring a small live view of tools into Claude. Starting today, where a connector supports it, you can open a tool beside your conversation or expand it to full screen, and ask Claude to work alongside you and make changes directly.

This is rolling out on the web and in the Claude desktop app on all plans, as part of the new Claude experience (opens in new tab) that brings chat and Cowork together. You’ll see these features once your account is updated with the new Claude or your organization turns it on.

What’s new:

  • Claude can work in your open tools. You can ask Claude to make changes to a page, row, or file that you have open and approve its actions the same way you approve a connector’s actions. Changes appear in the tool as Claude makes them, so you can keep working right alongside it.
  • The whole tool opens next to your conversation. You can work in the tool and hide the chat or go full screen when you need room. For tools like Confluence or Notion, that means you get the full editor, signed into your own account, rather than a limited preview.
  • Open a connected tool directly, without having to write a Claude prompt. When you want Claude’s help, you can ask from the same screen.
  • Pin the tools you use most. You can arrange them alongside your artifacts and access them with one click in your sidebar and the + menu.

Work with Claude in the tools you use

We’re starting with a small group of tools from our directory, including Asana, Canva, Carta, Dropbox, monday.com, Smartsheet, Vercel, and Webflow.

Here’s what you can do with some of the tools available in Claude today:

  • Adobe. Ask Claude to retouch, edit and add effects to photos; highlight, edit and redact PDFs.
  • Atlassian. Open a Confluence page beside your chat, ask Claude to write and edit, and review its changes live on the page.
  • Box. Open a Box file beside your chat, ask Claude to revise it, and compare the versions side by side before you keep the changes.
  • HubSpot. Prioritize pipeline tasks and follow-ups, then act on them in Claude.
  • Notion. Ask Claude to create a Notion doc or database. Build as you chat, or edit it yourself, without leaving Claude.

Figma, Harvey, and Shopify are also building integrations, and we encourage other developers to do the same.

For developers: built on MCP Apps

Interactive connectors run on MCP Apps, the open extension to the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) that lets an MCP server bring its own interface into AI applications. An MCP App you build isn’t limited to Claude and can run in any AI application that supports the extension (opens in new tab).

Until now, MCP Apps in Claude have mainly appeared as interactive views in the conversation. Claude now supports more of the extension, such as app tools, along with embedded sites, so a developer’s full app can run inside Claude.

Support for these capabilities is in public preview for developers. Developers can start building with them today. Read our docs (opens in new tab) to start building.

Getting started

You can connect the tools we mention above from the directory (opens in new tab), then open any tool from your chat or pin it to your sidebar.

For admins: If your organization already allows all of a connector’s tools, its new features appear as they roll out. Admins can restrict a connector’s tools the same way they do today.

item.title: How Curative is building a national provider network with ag…
item.description: Full title: How Curative is building a national provider network with agents on Claude
item.content:encoded:
In our series, How startups build with Claude, we highlight how startups are transforming their industries with AI. In this article, we share how Curative built a hierarchy of agents on Claude to sign provider contracts about 50 times faster than its team did in 2025.

The quick pitch
NameCurative
Founded2020; launched its health plan in 2022
FoundersFred Turner (CEO), Isaac Turner (CTO), Tami Wilson-Ciranna (President)
StackClaude Platform, Claude Code, bespoke claims system
Growth$150M Series B at a $1.275B valuation. 165,000+ members and 1,200+ employers (Dec 2025). 23,000 provider contracts signed with Gwen. 2,000 to 2,400 new contracts a week, up from 2,100 in all of 2025.

Curative sells health insurance to employers, with $0 copays and $0 deductibles for in-network care once members complete a Baseline Visit. Curative didn’t start out in insurance. It started as a lab startup and ended up processing 10% of all US COVID-19 tests according to their internal estimates. As a result, they started working with nearly every insurer in the country.

Its British founders, used to a system where patients don’t pay for care, saw inefficiencies and set out to build a payer focused on prevention. They realized they had significantly underestimated how hard building a national network would be.

“Sometimes naivety is good in startups, because you don’t know that it’s impossible. And then along the way you figure out a way to make it not impossible,” said Curative CEO Fred Turner. “Last year we signed 2,100 contracts, twice as many as we did the year before, but at 2,000 a year, we realized it would still be a 30-year build. There is a reason there are only a handful of national networks and they were all built about 30 years ago.”

Curative needed to accelerate contract signings, but hiring alone couldn’t close a gap that size.

Their solution: Gwen, an agent that works one provider deal from initial outreach to signature, surrounded by smaller agents that review its rates, check its messages, answer its questions, and escalate to humans for non-standard pricing.

Here is how they built it and what broke along the way.

Gwen: the provider contracts agent

Gwen works both inbound and outbound leads. Each run of Gwen handles a single provider, mostly on Claude Opus, so nothing from other deals influences it.

For example, if a practice fills in the form on Curative’s website, Gwen will research the practice and reply with proposed rates based on a purchased claims data set and price-transparency files payers are now required to publish. Gwen will show providers these market rate data to help with negotiations.

The rate reviewer runs on Sonnet. When Gwen wants to exceed its standard rate template, it writes out why, and the reviewer decides whether the rate makes sense.

“For a long time there was a big approval queue where Gwen had to get rates approved if she wanted to go a certain amount above the template, but we relaxed over time. Having a second agent review rates worked better than just giving Gwen more authority,” said Fred.

The Sonnet rate reviewer clears about two-thirds of Gwen’s requests and then anything non-standard goes to Fred for approval.

“The requests I see are from a big medical group or someone with a weird request that would come to me even if this wasn’t an agent-led motion,” said Fred.

Outbound deals take more persistence, because practices are busy. Some providers’ replies come after the fourteenth email and the ninth fax.

Image used with permission from Curative.

A judge, which runs on Haiku, reads every communication before it’s sent. Curative added it after Gwen copied providers on internal notes about how high it could go. A blocked message comes back with the reason, so Gwen can rewrite it and try again.

Each contract takes about 20 million tokens to complete, roughly a tenth of the original cost. These efficiencies enable one of Curative’s core strategies: signing smaller providers that have often been overlooked by larger networks.

“The agent will happily give you the same level of attention whether you are a large hospital system or if you’re a solo provider,” Fred explained. “From that agent’s perspective, this provider is its only focus.”

During negotiations, Gwen checks practice redlines against Curative’s policy document, then writes Python to merge both sides’ changes into a final document.

From form to signature, the process can be as quick as an hour. Once the contract is signed, a separate credentialing agent checks the provider’s licenses, and agents load the provider’s data and contract so claims can price against it.

Curative’s contracting team has grown from 45 to about 55 people since Gwen launched, each about 2.5 times as productive. They hand Gwen cold outreach and paperwork and take over warm leads by phone. Curative pays its contracting team on Gwen’s deals too, so people and agents share one target.

“People’s work becomes more about the relationship and less about paperwork,” said Fred.

Fred also believes faster contracting helps small practices stay independent. “If you start a medical practice and it takes three months to get in network and credentialed, you’re just not getting paid for three months,” he said.

Gwen is not Curative’s only agent. Brad, another Opus-based agent, helps sell Curative’s plan to employers, mainly through brokers. Brad follows up with brokers on each quote and helps underwriters move faster by pulling employee data out of the spreadsheets underwriters used to scrub by hand.

Using human-agent teams, Curative can now answer emailed or faxed claims disputes in under 30 minutes, with a letter specific to that claim. “Claims dispute responses used to take about 90 days and now take under 30 minutes by email or fax,” said Fred. “Most payers use a set of templates that are mail-merged together. That leaves a provider deeply unsatisfied, because usually the template doesn’t actually explain what’s going on. Now providers get a customized letter that explains the specifics of the individual claim, what’s happening, and why.”

All of their agents sit on bespoke claims, prior authorization, and finance systems that 13 engineers rebuilt this year with Claude Code. The team had once sized building a claims system alone at 100 engineer-years.

“We’re not trying to plug [these agents] into a claim system,” Fred said. “The claim system is Python running in AWS, and it has an MCP and it has an API, and Claude wrote it, so it understands it.”

What Curative learned from building agents that negotiate with people

Here’s what the Curative team learned about how to build agents that negotiate with people.

  • Start with one general tool. “We started off with, ‘Oh, we’ll have tools,’ and that doesn’t work that well, because redlining is quite complex,” Fred said. “What we found works best is that the model just has one tool, which is run Python, and it does all the redlining with a docx library. It works beautifully.”
  • Meet people on their channel. A fax tool more than doubled Gwen’s win rate. Many providers now handwrite on a printed fax and fax it back. “It’s meeting people where they are,” said Curative CTO Isaac Turner. “Yes, they have email, but really they’re comfortable in fax.”
  • Keep each run isolated. One Gwen run sees one provider and keeps no memory across deals. Brad, Curative’s sales agent, does keep memories, which works but needs care. “You can end up making notes that are wrong and then get into these doom loops, where it has a bad memory that can never be cleared,” Fred noted.
  • Improve the system from outside the run. Every few days, Fred gives Claude Code the same prompt: sample the last 10,000 runs, flag anything weird, and open a PR to fix it. “The improvement loops come from running Claude Code over lots of historic conversations and asking how could this have gotten better,” he said.
  • Experiment away from PHI first. For a long time Gwen was barred from protected health information (PHI), so early mistakes were in lower-risk settings. Where agents touch PHI now, back-end controls limit what enters a conversation, and agent activity is logged for audit. “We learned how to do it there and then transferred it over into PHI land,” said Fred. Signing Business Associate Agreements (BAAs), the contracts HIPAA requires before a vendor can handle PHI, has gotten easier too. “Anthropic especially has been very good about getting HIPAA-compliant versions of the latest services out very quickly,” said Isaac. “We’ve been able to onboard these new technologies very quickly despite it being regulated.”
  • Watch what the agent starts doing on its own and make sure it matches your risk profile. When providers asked for a flyer to share internally, Gwen made one with its Python tool, with no policy telling it to. When a front desk turned away a member at an in-network practice, Gwen asked the office to train its staff, then checked that the member got in.

Where Curative is going next

Next, Curative plans to bring agents to care navigation, extending the reach of the 130 people who guide and coach its members.

Fred expects agents on the provider side too. A large share of claims disputes already appear to be written by agents, and he hopes providers will use agents to negotiate contracts. “There’s a clearing price, and the faster you find the clearing price, everybody can get on with providing care,” he said.

Best practices from the Curative team
How much authority should an agent start with?Less than you think it can handle. Gwen began with a human approval queue for any rate above the template. Curative loosened the limits in steps and for more deterministic decisions, then added the rate reviewer, with Fred still approving what it doesn’t clear.
What happens when the agent gets it wrong?Plan for it, and compare it with the alternative. “The bar isn’t perfect,” Isaac said. “The bar is, if you had a thousand people signing contracts, how many mistakes would they make that you regret?”
How do you audit hundreds of thousands of messages?Log everything, put a judge agent on every outbound message, and have Claude Code sample the runs.

Start building with the Claude Platform today.

item.title: More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Inte…
item.description: Full title: More ways to work with Claude: Sheets, Whiteboards, and Interactive Connectors
item.content:encoded:
We've seen Claude Code change how developers work. Engineers went from manually coding line by line, to describing ideas and reviewing what Claude built. It reconnected them with the joy of building. Our goal is to bring that magic to every team, and today we're expanding what Claude makes possible. We're introducing new artifact types with Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data. We're also making it easier to work in your most-used apps with an upgrade to interactive connectors. Claude Meetings is coming soon.

All your connectors and context

In Claude Code, the context Claude needs is already in the codebase. For other teams, context sprawls across emails, apps, and drives. Claude reaches it through connectors built on the Model Context Protocol (opens in new tab) (MCP), the open standard we introduced for connecting AI to the tools you use. Claude Marketplace lists more than 9,000 connectors and plugins, including community-built ones.

Interactive connectors (opens in new tab) take this further. Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs. Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses.

Bring ideas to life faster, together

Starting today, Claude can build spreadsheets, whiteboards, and dashboards with your team. These work with its existing abilities to create documents, slide decks, and designs (opens in new tab), and with Claude Motion (opens in new tab) (beta), which helps you turn content into short animations. In each one, Claude quickly picks up what you need, so your thinking sets the pace of work:

  • New artifact types (opens in new tab):In Claude Sheets, your team and Claude build spreadsheets together, collaboratively organize data, create and edit formulas, and work across multiple tabs.Claude Whiteboards is a digital whiteboard that your team can use to lay out and organize ideas together in a meeting, then ask Claude to summarize the findings.Claude Data (formerly Dashboards) connects to tools like Snowflake and Salesforce and can use definitions your data team certifies (beta) to create dashboards, visual data stories, or narrated short videos.

You can also ask Claude to build custom artifacts for the way your team works, like an account tracker, a daily briefing, a project status board, or a contract review table. Since Claude carries the same context through every step, an idea can carry over from a whiteboard to a spreadsheet to a dashboard, without the need to reiterate the details.

Coming soon, Claude Meetings will let you add Claude to a call to take notes and update the documents your team is working on during the conversation.

Teams already working this way

Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers. Our legal team worked with Claude to build a Slack-based legal review tool that automatically draws redlines from the team’s own playbook. This brought marketing reviews from three days down to 24 hours, and easy fixes are made before a lawyer reviews the draft. Our finance team turned a long business update document for executives into an interactive page, and now the whole team updates it together with Claude.

Neither of these teams writes code, but they're experts in their fields. They used Claude to turn that knowledge into tools that saved them time, and that others can use. Our customers are working this way too:

“At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.”

Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer, Datadog

At Gusto, one member of the commercial legal team built a tool in a few hours that turns negotiated terms into signature-ready contracts. Turnaround went from over a week to hours, with that person still reviewing anything negotiated.

Gusto

“Claude and HubSpot work seamlessly together, so our CSMs have all the context they need to walk in prepared for every call. Live dashboards in Claude pull from HubSpot to show what matters for each call and which customers to reach out to next, and follow-up emails are drafted within 30 minutes of a call ending. Work that used to take hours every week now runs in the background, so our team can focus on helping customers build better solutions, prove value, and grow better.”

Jon Dick, Chief Customer Officer, Hubspot

“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”

Mindy Lok, Legal Chief Technology Officer, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Accenture

“Our FP&A team used to spend about 10 hours every forecast cycle on slides, commentary, and validation. We automated that assembly work in Claude and brought it down to under 30 minutes. Claude took all of that off our plate. Now we're doing what finance is supposed to do: finding the insight and driving the decision. That's a meaningful shift for a team supporting a business of this size.”

Ash Gupta, Director of Financial Planning and Analysis, Advantage Solutions

“At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.”

Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer, Datadog

At Gusto, one member of the commercial legal team built a tool in a few hours that turns negotiated terms into signature-ready contracts. Turnaround went from over a week to hours, with that person still reviewing anything negotiated.

Gusto

“Claude and HubSpot work seamlessly together, so our CSMs have all the context they need to walk in prepared for every call. Live dashboards in Claude pull from HubSpot to show what matters for each call and which customers to reach out to next, and follow-up emails are drafted within 30 minutes of a call ending. Work that used to take hours every week now runs in the background, so our team can focus on helping customers build better solutions, prove value, and grow better.”

Jon Dick, Chief Customer Officer, Hubspot

“At Accenture, Claude is helping us transform the way our legal teams work. We're excited about the opportunity to reimagine legal workflows and unlock new ways for our legal professionals to support our business.”

Mindy Lok, Legal Chief Technology Officer, Chief Intellectual Property Officer, Accenture

“Our FP&A team used to spend about 10 hours every forecast cycle on slides, commentary, and validation. We automated that assembly work in Claude and brought it down to under 30 minutes. Claude took all of that off our plate. Now we're doing what finance is supposed to do: finding the insight and driving the decision. That's a meaningful shift for a team supporting a business of this size.”

Ash Gupta, Director of Financial Planning and Analysis, Advantage Solutions

“At Datadog, Claude has extended from coding to knowledge work. Our product managers are using Claude to move from an idea to a feature brief, PRD, and testable prototype much faster, giving them more time to focus on customer needs, product judgment, and the right problems to solve. When someone builds something good with Claude at Datadog, it spreads fast.”

Yanbing Li, Chief Product Officer, Datadog

1/5

Built for and with enterprises

As Claude starts to connect to more tools, businesses need better ways to oversee its access and actions. We build in security and compliance controls to help enterprises meet their own requirements, and we use the same Claude for our own most sensitive work. On Enterprise plans, admins decide who can use which products and connectors, and set spend limits for the organization at a granular level.

That control applies to the tools Claude connects to. With Claude auto-connect (opens in new tab), now in beta on eligible Team and Enterprise plans, connecting an app like Notion, Atlassian, or Dropbox is a one-time setup. Employees are then connected to the tool the first time they use it in Claude, instead of connecting each one individually.

Whichever way a tool is connected, Claude works within your existing permissions. Admins can also limit what each connector does, meaning that Claude might be able to read Slack but not send messages on your behalf.

Protecting sensitive business data is core to how we build, and we're continuing to harden those protections as Claude takes on longer, more complex work:

  • Data from Enterprise organizations (opens in new tab) is encrypted in transit and at rest.
  • On Enterprise plans, security teams can see how Claude is being used (opens in new tab), through audit logs and a Compliance API that works with more than 100 security and compliance tools, including Splunk and CrowdStrike.
  • In the new Claude experience on Enterprise, each cloud session runs in its own isolated virtual machine (opens in new tab), with connector credentials kept outside it.

Work that keeps up with your ideas

Modern work is set up around software, but Claude works around you. It knows your team's work through the tools you connect, helps you bring ideas to life in the formats you need, and runs within the controls your admins set. That leaves you more time to focus and make progress on big goals.
