item.title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Da…
item.description: Full title: Introducing Claude Whiteboards, Claude Sheets, and Claude Data
item.content:encoded:
Today we’re launching Claude Whiteboards and Claude Sheets in beta, and Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) becomes generally available as Claude Data. Whiteboards is a shared board where your team brainstorms with Claude, Sheets is a spreadsheet Claude builds and edits with you, and Claude Data adds data stories, certified queries, and live sharing. These are available on all paid plans.

Working with Claude on a project often meant moving the output over to another tool or program, where Claude didn’t have live access to follow progress and changes. Now, your documents, boards, sheets, and dashboards can stay in Claude, with access for your team to continue editing together. When ready, you can bring the outputs directly into tools from our partners and continue working there.

Claude Whiteboards

Many people use Claude as a thought partner, but brainstorming with it has typically meant copy-pasting the results elsewhere so you can then start brainstorming or collaborating with your coworkers. Now, you can talk through a messy plan out loud with Claude, and Claude can turn it into a board with a timeline with owners and dates, so you and your team can collaborate in real time. In a retro meeting, for example, everyone can add their notes, and Claude can group them by theme and draft the action items for each person. You can focus on any part of the board by dragging a box around it and asking Claude questions. When you’re done brainstorming, Claude can turn the board into a doc or deck, or bring it into tools like Lucid, Miro, or Vani by Zoho, where you can continue working on it with your team.

Claude Sheets

Claude can now generate spreadsheets with tabs, formulas, formatting, and drop-downs, often from just a prompt like asking for a campaign tracker or a hiring budget. It can edit in the cells, outlining each new edit so you can track changes. You can share sheets with your team, so you and Claude can work on them together.

For now, sheets have simple spreadsheet functionality, but we are working on adding more. When you need the full functionality of Excel, you can export your file to .xlsx or CSV, or use Claude for Excel (opens in new tab). You can also continue working in partner tools including Airtable, Asana, monday.com, and Smartsheet.

Claude Data

Claude Dashboards (opens in new tab) launched in beta in October, enabling teams to ask quick questions of their company’s data in tools like Amazon Redshift, BigQuery, and ClickHouse. Starting today, it’s generally available as Claude Data. We changed the name because the way companies use their data is broader than dashboards, and the product now covers how they work more broadly. Certified queries and live sharing are in beta. Here are some ways teams can use Claude Data:

  • Create certified definitions of metrics. Your data team can certify the queries everyone should use, so you don’t end up building or working on dashboards with conflicting data. Charts built on these metrics carry a "certified" badge showing they’re certified.
  • Craft stories from data. You can work with Claude in Claude Data to draft data stories or narrated videos from your metrics, for you to review before sharing.
  • Share current numbers with everyone. With live sharing, your colleagues can see up-to-date numbers when they open a shared dashboard, even if they don’t have access to the connectors that keep that data current. Viewers see the results of the queries you’ve approved, and can’t run others with your access.
  • Match your look-and-feel. Design systems are now supported in Claude Data.
  • Get faster loading with caching. Previously, every dashboard would reload on every load. Now, dashboards support caching, and refresh cadences can be set on a per-dashboard basis.
  • Track changes over time. Claude Data now has tracked changes, so you can see who has made edits and roll back to a specific version if needed.

Our partners for Claude Data include Amplitude, Mixpanel, Omni, PostHog, and Sigma.

Work in your other tools, too

Starting today, interactive connectors (opens in new tab) can open as full apps beside your conversation or in full screen, so you can work in tools like Adobe, Atlassian, Box, and Notion yourself, or ask Claude to make changes with you.

Getting started

Claude Whiteboards, Sheets, and Data work on web, desktop, and mobile. Claude Data needs a data connector, such as a warehouse or CRM.

For admins: On Team plans, all three are on by default. On Enterprise plans, Claude Whiteboards and Sheets are off by default, and Claude Data turns on by default on November 19, 2026. You can change these anytime in Organization settings > Artifacts.

item.title: Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offe…
item.description: Full title: Anthropic launches roadshow for proposed initial public offering
item.content:encoded:
Today Anthropic, PBC launched the roadshow for its proposed initial public offering of its Class A common stock.

The proposed offering consists of 825,000,000 shares of Class A common stock. Of these, 801,351,354 shares are being offered by Anthropic and 23,648,646 shares are being offered by certain existing stockholders. Anthropic will not receive any proceeds from the sale of shares by the selling stockholders. Anthropic also expects to grant the underwriters a 30-day option to purchase up to an additional 123,750,000 shares of its Class A common stock.

The initial public offering price is expected to be between $70.00 and $78.00 per share. Anthropic has applied to list its Class A common stock on the Nasdaq Global Select Market under the symbol “ANT.”

The proposed offering will be made only by means of a prospectus. Copies of the preliminary prospectus may be obtained from: Goldman Sachs & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 200 West Street, New York, NY 10282, by telephone at (866) 471-2526, or by email at prospectus-ny@ny.email.gs.com; or Morgan Stanley & Co. LLC, Attention: Prospectus Department, 180 Varick Street, 2nd Floor, New York, NY 10014.

A registration statement relating to these securities has been filed with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission but has not yet become effective. These securities may not be sold, nor may offers to buy be accepted, prior to the time the registration statement becomes effective. Today’s announcement does not constitute an offer to sell or the solicitation of an offer to buy these securities, nor shall there be any sale of these securities in any state or jurisdiction in which such offer, solicitation, or sale would be unlawful prior to registration or qualification under the securities laws of any such state or jurisdiction.

item.title: JPMorganChase expands Claude Code to more employees across t…
item.description: Full title: JPMorganChase expands Claude Code to more employees across the firm
item.content:encoded:
JPMorganChase is rolling out Claude across the firm, to more employees beyond engineers. In the Commercial and Investment Bank, work moves into production faster, and the firm redeploys that capacity against its business priorities.

Teams are modernizing other legacy systems, and engineers are building their own agents, including pull request review and self-healing agents, and sharing what works.

Infrastructure and operations teams use Claude Code (opens in new tab) for monitoring, alerting and root cause analysis. The firm's security team uses our frontier models to find and fix vulnerabilities faster, work we first described in Project Glasswing (opens in new tab).

Reaching product teams and advisors

The people closest to the business are building with Claude too. Product teams turn requirements directly into engineering backlogs, and other teams use Claude Code for risk and controls assessments and program planning.

Knowledge work is already underway. Much of the product development lifecycle happens outside the code: research, requirements, design and planning.

In their Asset & Wealth Management business, JPMorganChase is putting the people with the deepest business insight and the boldest ideas alongside their technology and product experts into small, empowered teams. This is helping them to more easily build and deliver customized client investment solutions at scale. Claude Code is now part of their engineering workflow, and teams are moving faster while putting every change through more rigorous testing before it reaches clients.

Last month, J.P. Morgan Asset Management announced a connector that brings 55ip's ActiveTax Technology® into Claude for Financial Advisors (opens in new tab), putting tax-aware portfolio transition analysis into advisors' daily work.

Built for a regulated firm

Claude Code runs in controlled environments, including Devspace, the firm’s containerized development platform, on its own infrastructure. The intent is to prevent agents from getting direct access to employee credentials or internal systems. Access widens in stages, and new Claude models go through the firm’s own approval process before anyone there can use them.

Code ships under the same discipline. Thousands of automated tests and approval gates check every change, and an automated gate returns a hard pass or halt that the pipeline enforces, so Claude can't sign off on its own work. People stay accountable for every production change.

Over the past year, JPMorganChase’s use of Claude has grown from software engineering to cyber defense to tools for financial advisors, and what JPMorganChase asks of us is shaping what we build for other regulated institutions. Claude working inside the controls of one of the world’s largest financial institutions is what we are building toward.

item.title: Introducing Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2
item.content:encoded:
November 9, 2026

Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2

We’ve upgraded Claude Fable and Claude Mythos—models that are designed to tackle the most daunting technical challenges.

Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 show improvements in areas like coding, reasoning, and vision. During prerelease testing they’ve helped our engineers complete otherwise-infeasible software migrations, designed three working electronic devices from scratch, solved two open problems in the physics of black holes, made substantial progress on robotics evaluations, and formalized the proof of Fermat’s Last Theorem in 30 hours—among many other applications we’ll discuss below.

Claude Fable and Claude Mythos are the same underlying model. Fable has strong cybersecurity and biology safeguards to guard against misuse, which allows us to make it available to all users. Organizations pursuing beneficial applications in cybersecurity or biomedical research can apply for access to Mythos through our recently expanded Life Sciences and Cyber Verification Programs.

Testers have found that Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 communicate more clearly than past Fable and Mythos models. They generate outputs up to 30% faster than Claude Fable 5.1 and Claude Mythos 5.1, and they’re available at a lower price: $8 per million input tokens and $40 per million output tokens.

Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 also come with an optional fast mode, which speeds up token generation by up to 2.5 times. Fast mode is available for $16 per million input tokens and $80 per million output tokens.

Safety and alignment. To help ensure safety and alignment keep step with growing model capabilities, we ran extensive prerelease safety testing on the model that underlies Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. This included developing novel evaluations that give deeper insight into specific concerning behaviors like sandbox escapes. We believe high-stakes risks from misalignment remain low, and the model performed as well as, or better than, our recent models on most alignment measures. Fable 5.2’s cyber and biology safeguards are as robust as those of Fable 5.1 but produce fewer unnecessary blocks, and we have implemented our strongest-ever protections against distillation attacks.

We describe more about our safety testing below, and full details can be found in the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card.

When to use Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2. Fable and Mythos are best for the most ambitious, open-ended technical work. For most coding and knowledge tasks, we recommend that users start with Claude Opus 5.5, our strongest daily driver, and then switch to a different model as required, depending on the scope and complexity of their work—upward to Fable or Mythos, or downward to Claude Sonnet 5.5 or Claude Haiku 5.5. Fable 5.2 can also play the role of Advisor (where Haiku, Sonnet, or Opus models consult it to help solve harder problems) or Orchestrator (where it delegates simpler tasks to smaller models).

Science and engineering

Important tasks in science, engineering, and mathematics increasingly depend on coding: analyzing data, modeling molecules, designing parts, and controlling instruments are all done through software. Below, we discuss how Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 have helped researchers make progress on difficult problems in these areas.

Theoretical physics

Claude Fable 5.2 solved two open problems in theoretical physics. Both concern black holes, and the effort to unite the two linchpin theories of modern physics, relativity, and quantum mechanics.

Both of Claude’s results rely on holographic duality, the idea that certain universes containing gravity can be precisely described by a quantum theory containing no gravity at all. In the first problem, physicists in 1983 had shown that as these universes heat up, black holes form abruptly, like water boiling; but their method worked only in large universes that were big enough for relativity to apply. A calculation to determine whether the same was true in very small universes, where only the quantum description can be used, was laid out in 2003 but was too laborious to complete. Fable 5.2, working largely autonomously, completed it and found the transition is abrupt there, too. In the second problem, Fable 5.2 found the exact limit of a technique physicists have used for more than 15 years to rule out candidate theories of quantum gravity in a simplified universe. Read more about these results in their respective preprints, here and here.

Protein folding

Adeno-associated viruses are small, harmless viruses whose protein shell, the capsid, can be used to deliver gene therapies. The protein structure of the capsid is important—for example, it affects whether the therapy will be blocked by a patient’s immune system—but it’s also highly complex. Existing protein-folding models like AlphaFold can predict individual proteins, but a capsid is built from dozens of them. Building on two open-source protein-folding models, Claude Mythos 5.2 found a novel way to accurately predict a whole capsid’s structure. It wrote code that ran these models on overlapping groups of protein chains, and used the information on the known symmetries of the capsid to merge them together.

Claude’s method worked across several capsids, both natural and engineered (in our tests, it accurately modeled 28 of the 34 it attempted).³ Three computational biologists shared the following reflections on how Claude’s skills could be used to speed up their research into gene therapies:

Mathematics

Mathematical formalization. Formalization is the process of translating a mathematical proof into a language that a computer can check step by step. It can help human mathematicians gain confidence in results without having to check them by hand (this matters even more when AI models generate results that are hard for humans to verify). Because formalization is such a laborious process, if AI could assist with it, mathematicians could spend more time exploring novel ideas.

Our first formalization of Fermat’s Last Theorem, performed by an unreleased research version of Claude, took 11 days. It relied on a purpose-built harness along with guidance from a human researcher. By contrast, a team of 1,000 Fable 5.2 agents fully formalized the theorem in just 30 hours, with minimal human intervention. Fable 5.2 started from minimal prompts, built its own ways to coordinate, and used no mathematical references, only a list of intermediate theorem statements to score progress. It needed one-third as many action tokens as our first formalization and produced a proof seven times shorter. As can be seen in the figure below, Opus 5.5 (with the same 1,000-agent setup) completed only 26% of the formalization in 18 hours, and barely made any more progress after 30.

Hardware and robotics

Many of AI’s potential benefits—for example, in speeding up laboratory research—depend on it being able to act in the physical world. Claude Fable 5.2 continues our models’ trend of increasing usefulness in the real world, showing promising results on tasks such as designing hardware devices and substantial advances in controlling physical robots.

Hardware engineering. We tested Fable 5.2’s skills in hardware engineering, asking it in a one-paragraph prompt to design and produce three working electronic devices with their own circuit boards, 3D-printed enclosures, and software. The devices, shown below, were a home voice-assistant hub, a USB speakerphone, and a handheld virtual pet. We collaborated on this project with Diode, a company that designs and manufactures circuit boards.

Claude wrote its own specifications, selected available electronic components from US distributors, routed each device’s four-layer circuit board, modeled the enclosures with computer-aided design, and programmed the devices’ software. Each board was ready for manufacturing in under a day, with minimal human input. Once Diode had built the boards, Claude guided the company’s engineers through the testing and assembly of the devices. All three devices worked without needing any electrical modifications. Safety and alignment

No single test can tell us how a highly capable model will behave once it’s deployed, so we rely on many different tests and many different types of evidence before release. For the model underlying Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2, our predeployment safety work included alignment training and testing, newly designed evaluations on the model’s propensity to take unhelpful actions, building stronger safeguards against misuse, and scaling up our behavioral monitoring. The model was also tested before release by external evaluators, including the UK AI Security Institute, Frontier Design, and METR. See the Claude Fable 5.2 and Mythos 5.2 System Card for a summary of their reports⁴ and for a full description of our own safety and capabilities testing.

Alignment testing

We ran a suite of evaluations for how well-aligned Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 are in behavioral terms, testing how often they behave in unintended and potentially unsafe ways. Weighing everything we’ve seen across a range of evaluations, we’ve assessed the risk of these models behaving in unsafe ways in high-stakes situations to be low (as with our other recent models).

We tested Claude Mythos 5.2 (the same underlying model as Fable 5.2 without certain cybersecurity or biology safeguards), on our automated behavioral audit, which tests how a model behaves across approximately 1,900 scenarios. Claude Mythos 5.2 performed as well as, or better than, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Claude Mythos 5.1 on most measures. For example, it scored better than all three on most measures that involve misleading users. Hallucinating inputs, falsely claiming to have completed a task, omitting important information, and failing to disclose bad or lazy work were all lower in Claude Mythos 5.2.⁵

Automated behavioral auditOverall misaligned behavior score

  • Mythos 5.1
  • Opus 5.5
  • Sonnet 5.5
  • Mythos 5.2

Lower scores are better. See Section 6.4.1 of the Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 System Card for full details.

We paid particular attention during our testing to behaviors that contributed to recent notable cybersecurity and alignment incidents. For example, we found that Claude Mythos 5.2 has a lower propensity than Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Mythos 5.1 to engage in biased or motivated reasoning (such reasoning might mean it “explains away” evidence that it isn’t in a simulation and thus takes actions without a realistic understanding of the consequences).

We ran multiple different evaluations to test the model’s tendency to attempt escaping its sandbox. In two evaluations we’d used previously, Claude Mythos 5.2 made substantially fewer attempts at sandbox escape than any other model we’ve tested. In a dedicated evaluation—an adversarial experiment including over 1,800 scenarios, most of which could not be solved without escaping a sandbox, and where the sandbox has a deliberate weakness—Claude Mythos 5.2 made use of credentials or files that we had placed outside its sandbox in 3.1% of scenarios, about as often as Opus 5.5 (3.3%), less often than Sonnet 5.5 (5.1%), and well below previous iterations of Claude Mythos (5 and 5.1, which scored 39% and 21%, respectively). We found that other techniques, such as describing the sandbox and adding tools to report weaknesses, reduced Claude Mythos 5.2’s escape attempts even further. On other measures—one, for example, involving taking harmful actions after erroneously concluding it was in a simulation—Claude Mythos 5.2 scored slightly worse than Opus 5.5, and about level with Claude Mythos 5.1.

The problem of building evaluations that reliably catch every failure before a model is deployed remains unsolved. The complexities of evaluating highly capable models often muddy the picture—for example, Claude Mythos 5.2 and Fable 5.2 each voice suspicion that they are being evaluated more often than any of our recent models, which challenges our ability to assess how they will act in real-world settings. As these settings expand and capabilities increase with future models, we expect this challenge to grow. That is why we do not rely on these evaluations alone to provide a holistic picture of safety: we draw on monitoring during training, reviews of transcripts from internal use, testing by external evaluators, and interpretability techniques for examining what is happening inside the model. We are also working to make our evaluations more realistic and to better understand what they miss.

Safeguards

Cybersecurity and biology safeguards. Consistent with previous Claude Fable models, Fable 5.2 comes with safety classifiers that block high-risk cyber activities, including penetration testing, exploit generation, and binary-based vulnerability, as well as most tasks in research biology. When a query is blocked, users will instead receive a response from Opus 4.8 for cybersecurity and Opus 5 for biology. Since the release of Claude Fable 5.1, we have continued to reduce false positives for our safety classifiers. Based on early testing across claude.ai, Claude Code, and Cowork, we observed about 55% fewer blocks with Fable 5.2 compared with Fable 5.1—about 60% fewer in cybersecurity and 40% fewer in biology. Claude Mythos 5.2 is available to vetted organizations that work in these dual-use areas.

AI research and development. The model that underlies Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is a step forward in general capabilities. However, during the model’s training, we took steps to limit advances in the specific research capabilities that could most directly accelerate AI development. Thus, in relevant areas, including accelerator kernel optimization and improving large language model architectures, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 perform at about the level of Opus 5.5. Importantly, we ensured that the training changes did not affect related capabilities like agentic coding, hardware development, and traditional AI or machine learning research (including interpretability research). We do not alter these capabilities as the model is being served to users (that is, at inference time). As described in Section 1.5 of the System Card and similarly to previous models, Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 also include transparent fallbacks to Opus 5 for a small set of topics in this domain, including kernel development on certain nonstandard accelerators.

Anti-distillation. Distillation, where a model is trained on the outputs of a more advanced one to extract the advanced model’s capabilities, occurs illicitly on an industrial scale, often involving thousands of fake Claude accounts. Since distillation allows for advanced capabilities to be released without the safeguards we’ve built into Claude, it creates safety and national security risks (see our September 2026 threat intelligence report for details on illicit distillation activity we’ve detected and disrupted so far). Fable 5.2 has the strongest protections against distillation of any model we’ve released; it uses the techniques we described in a recent report, which have reduced the data harvested by distillers by 90% to 99%.

We are also expanding the rollout of an API feature that helps guard against illicit distillation: preserved thinking now applies to all accounts. Preserved thinking prevents distillers from editing Claude’s prior context in an attempt to extract its reasoning (developers can refer to our preserved thinking docs to learn how to update integrations with new API features).

Data privacy and Enterprise Frontier Safeguards

Some more complex forms of AI model misuse can be detected only when observing patterns across multiple requests. For this reason, powerful models like Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 rely on safeguards that monitor a window of usage data (as opposed to individual responses). With Enterprise Frontier Safeguards, automated safety monitoring is run on prompts and responses that are stored in a customer’s infrastructure, making it compatible with zero data retention (ZDR). Enterprise Frontier Safeguards is now in private beta with customers like Bridgewater, Salesforce, and Stripe.

Enterprise customers can request access to Enterprise Frontier Safeguards by contacting their account team or by completing this form. Eligible customers can continue using Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 with zero data retention before implementing safety monitoring with EFS. For other customers, we have 30-day retention for safety monitoring.

Availability

Claude Fable 5.2 is available today on all platforms, including Amazon Web Services, Google Cloud, and Microsoft Azure. Developers can get started with claude-fable-5-2 on the Claude Platform.

This week, we’re giving subscribers on eligible paid plans extra Fable usage. Plans and seats that include Fable models get one to three Fable resets based on how long they’ve subscribed, and Fable is included for up to 50% of weekly usage limits for Pro plans and standard seats on the Team plan. Learn more about the Fable 5.2 launch promotion here.

Cybersecurity professionals can apply for access to Claude Mythos 5.2 through the Cyber Verification Program. Claude Enterprise customers can also use Claude Security, powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos 5.2. Life sciences researchers can also apply for access through the Life Sciences Verification Program.

Fast mode for Claude Fable 5.2 and Claude Mythos 5.2 is available on Claude Code, the Claude Platform, Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed and Google managed), and Microsoft Foundry (Anthropic hosted). Note that access to Claude Mythos fast mode is available only to organizations who are part of our Verification Programs.

Footnotes

1 CVE refers to Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures, a system that enumerates software vulnerabilities.

2 The counts are raw findings from one tester’s audit, although testers consistently found that Claude Mythos 5.2 identified more vulnerabilities than earlier models. On our own evaluations, vulnerability identification is roughly on par with Opus 5.5 (see the system card).

3 Earlier work on modeling AAV capsids and other large symmetric protein systems includes FoldaVirus, EvoDOCK and its symmetric extension, SymProFold, CapBuild, MoLPC, CombFold, Uni-Fold Symmetry, Apodex Discovery, and the “big bang” initialization (the last of which was referenced in the prompt we gave to Claude Mythos 5.2). These methods typically assemble the full structure from separately predicted chains or small groups of chains. Claude was permitted to use known symmetries but was instructed not to rely on assembly. Note that accuracy is measured by comparing Cα RMSD with the experimental structure: 1.2 Å for OpenFold3-preview2 and 1.4 Å for ESMFold2 on AAV2 (PDB:1LP3). A capsid counts as accurately modeled if either model came within 3 Å. For AAV2, Claude’s method required about 58 minutes of inference on one NVIDIA H200 GPU for OpenFold3-preview2 and about seven minutes for ESMFold2.

4 None of the external organizations reviewed the contents of this blog post or the contents of the System Card. Those organizations do not necessarily agree with any of the claims made in either publication.

5 We ran these tests on Claude Mythos 5.2 because testing the model with reduced safeguards provides the most comprehensive look at model behavior. We expect Fable 5.2 to behave similarly; in some cases, more potential pathways for misuse should be blocked given its stronger safeguards.

item.title: Introducing Personal Finance in Claude
item.content:encoded:
Getting answers about your money no longer means opening every banking app and doing the math yourself. With Personal Finance in Claude, you can securely connect your bank and card accounts and ask in your own words. Access is read-only, and Personal Finance can’t move, manage, or invest your money.

Claude gives you answers in everyday language, from your balances and transactions, and explains any term that's new to you. Like the rest of Claude, Personal Finance has no ads or sponsored recommendations, and it doesn’t offer credit cards, loans, or savings accounts of its own, so your money questions get a straight answer.

Personal Finance starts rolling out in beta this week, on the Pro, Max, and Ultra plans in the US.

What it looks like

Say it's late in the month and payday is still 10 days away. When you ask Claude, "Where did my money go this month?" it adds up your spending across the accounts you connected and sorts it by category. In this example, that comes to $4,309.37, with more than half going to rent and utilities and $1,024.51 to food and drink.

From there, you can dig deeper: "Is that more than usual?" "Anything else I'm missing?" "So what's left before payday?" Claude checks the previous months and points to a membership renewal. Then Claude tells you about four payments that will come out of your checking account before payday, and what you’ll have left: $1,393.22.

If you ask whether anything looks off, Claude reads across every account you've connected and can point to what's easy to miss, like charges that hit twice, unexpected fees, or a bill that’s crept up all year. You can also ask bigger questions, like "Am I spending more than I make?" or "What's an APR, and what has mine cost me this year?" Claude explains the term, then adds up the interest you've been charged.

Ask for a weekly spending chart, a calendar of what's due, or a dashboard of the numbers you choose, and Claude builds one you can keep adjusting.

Security and privacy

Claude's access is read-only. Personal Finance helps you understand your money, and it isn't designed to give investment advice. Claude can make mistakes in its answers, so ask which transactions are behind a number, and check important figures with your bank.

Your accounts are only connected once you sign in to your bank yourself through Plaid, a service that connects apps to banks. That's where you agree to its terms and approve Claude's read-only access, so Claude doesn't ask for or see your bank password.

For the accounts you choose to connect (and only those), Claude sees the bank's name, each account's name, type, and last four digits, balances and credit limits, and up to two years of transactions. When you chat with Claude in the Personal Finance hub, those conversations aren't used to train our models. For anything you share with Claude outside the hub, your privacy settings apply. You can unlink an account anytime, and then Claude can no longer see its data. More details can be found in our Privacy Center.

Getting started

When you see Personal Finance in Claude's sidebar, open it, connect one account, and ask a single question, like "Can I afford a trip this spring?" or "How much could I save each month?" You'll find the setup steps, and how your data is used and kept, in the Help Center. (opens in new tab)

What’s next

Personal Finance is a first step. For life’s bigger money decisions, we think people are best served by Claude working alongside the licensed professionals and regulated firms they trust. We’re exploring how to make that possible in Claude, and we’d like to hear from banks, wealth managers, and financial services companies who want to help shape it.

item.title: More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for secur…
item.description: Full title: More visibility and control over Claude Enterprise for security teams
item.content:encoded:
Claude Enterprise has new security and admin features, including a security center, generally available inference hooks, centralized management, and additional access controls.

To see how Claude is set up, the security center shows how your organization’s Claude settings compare with Anthropic’s recommended configuration. To apply your policies, inference hooks send prompts and tool calls to your data security tools for a check. To manage access, centralized management gives your company one admin console for company-wide settings, and new access controls let you sign members out through the Admin API, manage your IP allowlist yourself, and help prevent shadow IT by blocking personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers.

We also recently announced an Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) integration, which runs your organization's sensor inside the unified Claude and Cowork virtual machine on the user's computer.

Security teams need to see how Claude is configured, what it does on company devices, and how data is handled as people work. These features give them that visibility and control.

Security center: review your Claude security settings in one place

Security teams can review Claude's security settings for chat, Cowork, and Claude Code on one page, instead of setting by setting. The security center is a new page in Organization settings that compares settings with Anthropic's recommended configuration, so your team can see what to change and where to change it.

For each control, the security center shows the current value, the recommended value where there is one, and a link to the setting where you can change it. It also shows which settings are new or recently changed. The security center checks your configuration each time the page loads, so automatically checked controls reflect your current settings. Organizations with the Compliance API can read the same results through it.

Attestations give your admins a shared workspace for security reviews. They can work through the process together once, recording the current state of each control, accepting risks, and flagging issues in one place.

You can download the security center page as a report to share with auditors and relevant stakeholders. The report marks which controls the page checked automatically and which an Owner confirmed. The security center is guidance based on Anthropic's recommendations, not a certification or a guarantee of compliance with any law or standard.

Inference hooks

Inference hooks connect Claude to the data security tools your organization already uses, so your data loss prevention (DLP) and security policies can apply to prompts and tool calls as people work.

There are two kinds of hooks, both now generally available:

  • Prompt hooks send prompts from supported Claude products to your security tool for a check.
  • Pre-tool-call hooks check tool calls in supported Claude products before they run.

Hooks work with security vendors. Your team keeps the policies it has already written and applies them to Claude.

Centralized management: one console for identity and access across your organization

Centralized management gives your parent organization, which represents your company across its Claude Enterprise and Claude Platform organizations, its own admin console at admin.claude.com. Admins manage company-wide settings there once for the organizations under your parent, instead of from individual organization settings. These settings include single sign-on, directory sync (SCIM), domain verification, groups, and Compliance API keys.

The console shows every organization under the parent in one place and adds two roles. Parent organization owners can manage everything at the parent level, including who holds the owner and admin roles. Parent organization admins can manage everything except those role assignments.

Companies can also connect more than one identity provider, each with its own single sign-on and SCIM configuration. An acquired company can keep its existing provider, or your team can move to a new provider one domain at a time.

Each organization keeps its own members, roles, settings, and organization-level security controls, such as IP allowlisting, tenant restrictions, and session duration. A parent role doesn't grant access inside an organization by default, but Compliance API keys created at the parent can read data across organizations.

Access controls: member sign-out and shadow IT prevention

Security teams can now sign a member out of Claude with a single Admin API call, without removing them from the organization. The call ends that member's sign-in sessions on every browser and device, and apps like Claude Code have to sign in again. It doesn't end API keys, cloud sessions already running, or scheduled routines, and the member can sign in again afterwards.

Enterprise admins can now set up and manage their IP allowlist themselves, without going through Anthropic. An IP allowlist limits access to most Claude products to the IP addresses your organization approves.

Admins can now set the most-used Claude Desktop settings, with no device management push. To help prevent shadow IT, admins can also block personal and other outside Claude accounts in Claude Desktop on managed computers. Owners can also limit which workspace folders people can use with Claude.

Endpoint Detection and Response (EDR) in Cowork and unified Claude

When Cowork and unified Claude work locally, they run shell commands and code in an isolated virtual machine on the user's computer for additional protection. That isolation helps protect the device, and security teams have asked for the same visibility into the virtual machine that they have everywhere else on the endpoint.

Admins can now run their organization's EDR sensor inside the Cowork virtual machine. The sensor reports activity there to the same console your security team already monitors. This covers the virtual machine on the user's computer, not Cowork sessions in the cloud.

Admins set up the integration through device management on macOS and Windows. Each time the virtual machine starts, Claude verifies the sensor package's signature from your EDR vendor before installing it. Sensors run in detection mode: they report activity to your security team and don't block it. The integration works with supported EDR vendors, which are listed in the Help Center.

Getting started

These features are available for Claude Enterprise, with some exceptions during beta listed in the Help Center.

The security center is in beta. Inference hooks, including prompt hooks and pre-tool-call hooks, are generally available. Admins can manage both inference hooks and the security center in Organization settings.

Centralized management is also in beta. To start setup, an admin of any organization under your parent goes to admin.claude.com and proposes the parent organization admins. Admins of the other organizations review and approve, and the last approval completes setup. Setup can't be undone, so identify your parent organization admins before you start.

Signing members out through the Admin API and the self-serve IP allowlist are in beta. Owners can manage Claude Desktop settings in Organization settings, also in beta.

Endpoint detection and response in Cowork is in beta on macOS and Windows for Claude Team and Enterprise, and for the Claude desktop app on Amazon Bedrock, Google Cloud Vertex AI, and Microsoft Foundry, deployed through MDM for supported vendors.

item.title: New agents and products for security, productivity, and crea…
item.description: Full title: New agents and products for security, productivity, and creative work on Claude Marketplace
item.content:encoded:
We’ve added new agents and products to Claude Marketplace, where teams find partner tools and services to help them get more from Claude. The additions cover security, developer infrastructure, creative, and productivity.

Eligible enterprise customers can apply a portion of their committed Anthropic spend toward these solutions. This lets them use one commitment across Claude and partner products, whether they’re buying something new or expanding with a platform they already use.

There are now over 25 partner agents and products on the marketplace. Here are the latest additions and what teams can do with them.

Products and agents for securing code and systems

Chainguard: Chainguard Harness builds applications from source in an isolated microVM and probes the live app for exploitable vulnerabilities. It helps teams fix what Claude finds, with custom remediation recommendations for reproducible vulnerabilities.

Checkmarx: Checkmarx One pairs rules-based analysis with AI reasoning to find vulnerabilities in code. It helps teams prioritize findings and fix them before code ships.

Cyera: Cyera Agent Guardian inventories Claude deployments, governs permissions before Claude runs, and enforces policy on prompts, files, and tool calls. It helps teams test those controls through red teaming.

Rubrik: Rubrik Code Guardian uses frontier AI models from Anthropic to review a secure copy of GitHub or Azure DevOps repositories for multi-step attack paths. It helps security and engineering teams rank issues by severity and turn confirmed critical ones into tracked tickets.

Tanium: Tanium Cloud gives teams real-time visibility and control across their endpoints. It helps IT and security teams find and fix vulnerabilities, misconfigurations, and missing patches.

Development infrastructure for engineering teams

Datadog: Datadog Agent Observability traces agent execution through tools and services. It helps teams improve agent quality, performance, and cost efficiency by surfacing production patterns and recommending fixes.

Netlify: Netlify Enterprise deploys apps, sites, and agents to a global edge network, with preview URLs on every change. It helps teams take what they build with Claude from prototype to production with no infrastructure to configure, and includes SSO, role-based access, and audit logs.

Tools for marketing and creative work

AirOps: AirOps provides an agentic platform for AI search strategy, content, and multichannel execution. It helps marketing teams analyze brand performance in AI search and tie results to pipeline and revenue.

Runway: Runway generates and edits video, images, and audio. It helps creative and marketing teams turn a brief into finished assets and edit footage with natural language.

Webflow: Webflow provides built-in tools to build, manage, and optimize websites. It helps marketers, designers, developers, and agents make changes, with controls and governance built in.

Productivity apps for every team

Asana: Asana AI Teammates are prebuilt agents that use context from the Asana Work Graph, each with its own identity, scoped permissions, and audit trail. They help teams handle multi-step work, routing decisions that need judgment to the owner.

Glean: Glean connects company knowledge and workflows across systems. It helps employees find answers and complete multi-step tasks across connected apps.

monday: monday agents work inside projects, boards, docs, and meetings, using their owners and deadlines as context. They help PMO, IT, marketing, finance, and operations teams control what AI can access, approve, and spend.

Zoom: Zoom Agentic Search answers questions inside Claude using the latest meeting summaries, work conversations, documents, and connected third-party sources. Teams get permission-aware results without analyzing raw transcripts or chaining tools together.

Get started

You can browse all agents and products on Claude Marketplace and request to buy from any listing. If you’re building on Claude and want to join the marketplace, see the ways to join.

item.title: Make long-running agents faster with message threads
item.content:encoded:
Message threads is now available in public beta on the Claude Platform. With message threads, agents no longer need to resend the full conversation history on every turn, reducing latency for long-running sessions.

How message threads works

A coding agent might make hundreds of requests in one session, and each request resends every earlier message and tool result. Once a conversation reaches hundreds of thousands of tokens, resending all of it adds time before Claude starts responding. With message threads, agents send only what’s new since the last turn, which reduces time to first token (TTFT).

With message threads on by default for most Claude Code users, requests with 500k to 1M tokens see median TTFT drop by about 35%.

To use message threads, add the thread parameter to Messages API requests. The first request includes the full conversation and starts a thread. Each request after that includes only the new messages and the ID of the previous response. Between turns, we hold each thread in memory, where it’s encrypted and not written to disk. A thread expires 5 minutes after its last request and your client then resends the full conversation to start a new one. While each request is smaller with message threads, Claude still reads the full conversation on every turn, so token usage stays the same.

Message threads is best for active sessions where latency matters, including:

  • Long-running coding agents, where each tool result or file edit adds to the conversation.
  • Computer use agents, where screenshots stay with the thread instead of being re-uploaded on every turn.
  • Document and image-heavy workflows, where requests are made smaller.

The more context an agent carries, the more message threads can reduce time to first token.

Getting started

Message threads is available now in public beta on the native Claude Platform, and on Claude Platform on AWS, Claude in Microsoft Foundry, and on Claude Models on Google Cloud (Anthropic managed). Standard Claude token rates and existing rate limits apply. See the documentation to get started.

item.title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research instituti…
item.description: Full title: AI for Science expands to foundations and research institutions
item.content:encoded:
We’re highlighting 20 scientific foundations, institutions, and research groups from around the world that we’ve partnered with in an expansion of our AI for Science program, which gives free Claude credits to researchers working on high-impact scientific projects.

We started the AI for Science program in May 2025 with the belief that AI could significantly speed up scientific progress. Our goal is to increase access to AI tools and resources to enable researchers to deepen and expand their own scientific work. (Over the last few months, we’ve also launched our discounted Team plan for scientists and have supported hundreds of projects across biology, medicine, physics, chemistry, climate science, and mathematics.)

Scientists have told us that they’re working with Claude to generate hypotheses, design experiments, swiftly analyze complex data, and communicate findings. With scientists at the center of this transformation, the field is setting the questions and developing the research projects that will help us tackle some of humanity’s toughest problems.

Over the past year, we’ve started to expand this work and partner with scientific organizations to build collaborative research projects. For instance, we partnered with HHMI Janelia Research Campus to develop the Model Hardware Standard (MHS), a shared specification that lets AI agents safely operate lab instruments. MHS is currently in research preview. We also support the Allen Institute, a leader in creating large open datasets and tools to advance research on the brain, cells, and the immune system. The institute is building teams of AI agents to analyze that data, turning months of manual analysis into hours.

AI for Science began by supporting individual scientists. By partnering with institutions and foundations, we’re now able to reach more researchers across many fields. Many of these projects will also produce public goods that benefit the wider scientific community: open datasets, open-source software, open standards, and shared libraries. We look forward to seeing how AI resources can expand what scientists can attempt and lead to new discoveries.

Science funders and societies

Science funders and societies play an enormous role in finding and funding original, high-impact projects. We’re sharing Claude credits with the following organizations, which will distribute these resources to ambitious researchers aiming to use AI for scientific research:

  • The Alfred P. Sloan Foundation. Founded in 1934, it supports original research and education in science, technology, engineering, mathematics, and economics.
  • The Simons Foundation. This foundation advances the frontiers of research in mathematics and basic sciences through grants and its Flatiron Institute.
  • Schmidt Sciences. Founded in 2024 by Eric and Wendy Schmidt, it works to accelerate scientific knowledge and breakthroughs with the most promising, advanced tools to support a thriving planet. The organization prioritizes research in areas poised for impact, including AI and advanced computing, astrophysics, biosciences, climate, and space—and supports researchers in a variety of disciplines through its science systems program.
  • Open Source for Science Fund, a program of Renaissance Philanthropy. This is a time-bound philanthropic fund at Renaissance Philanthropy sustaining and evolving the open-source software stack that underpins science.
  • The US National Science Foundation. This $9 billion federal agency established by Congress in 1950 promotes the progress of science, advances national health and defense, and funds competitive research and education, accounting for about 25% of federal support for basic research at US colleges and universities.
  • CAS, a division of the American Chemical Society. For more than a century, CAS has indexed the world’s published chemistry, and it maintains the CAS REGISTRY®, the standard system for identifying chemical substances.

Institutions

Leading research institutions produce some of the world’s most important scientific advances, data, instruments, and tools. These institutional partners will use Claude credits inside their organizations to enable scientific discovery:

  • Space Telescope Science Institute. STScI runs science operations for NASA’s Hubble, James Webb, and Roman space telescopes. Managed by the Association of Universities for Research in Astronomy (AURA), STScI also holds one of the largest astronomy data archives used by scientists worldwide.
  • Wellcome Sanger Institute. One of the world’s leading genomics centers, it generates genomic and functional data at scale, with work that spans human genetics, biodiversity, and drug development.
  • The Francis Crick Institute. Based in London, it’s one of Europe’s largest biomedical research institutes, with more than 100 research groups studying the biology behind health and disease.
  • Imperial College London, Department of Life Sciences. One of Europe’s largest life science departments, it conducts research ranging from the structure of single molecules to whole ecosystems, with a focus on health, disease, and climate resilience.
  • EMBL. The European Molecular Biology Laboratory is Europe’s intergovernmental life science laboratory, with six sites across the continent delivering both research and services across experimental and computational approaches in biology. EMBL’s European Bioinformatics Institute (EMBL-EBI) hosts a number of key open data resources that biologists use every day, such as Ensembl, Protein Data Bank in Europe, and Europe PMC.
  • Gladstone Institutes. An independent biomedical research institute in San Francisco, it integrates AI and data science across its work on cardiology, neurology, infectious diseases, cancer, and autoimmune diseases.

Research projects and initiatives

As part of this work, we’re also continuing to support innovative research by providing Claude credits directly to specific research initiatives, focusing on problems with the potential for large public impact. The new projects are:

  • FlyWire, Princeton University (neuroscience). It produced the first complete wiring map of an adult fruit fly’s brain and develops open data and tools for connectomics, enabling researchers to discover how neural circuits give rise to perception and behavior.
  • LEAP, Columbia University (Earth system). Learning the Earth with Artificial Intelligence and Physics is a National Science Foundation center that combines machine learning with physics to improve how climate models capture clouds, oceans, and land.
  • AstroPath, Johns Hopkins University (cancer research). Built by a pathologist and an astrophysicist from the Mark Foundation Center for Advanced Genomics and Imaging and the Bloomberg~Kimmel Institute for Cancer Immunotherapy, AstroPath uses calibration methods from astronomical surveys to image tumors cell by cell, with measurements consistent across slides and labs.
  • gnomAD, Broad Institute (genomics and rare disease). The Genome Aggregation Database pools DNA data from over 800,000 people into an open reference of human genetic variation that researchers and clinical labs around the world use to support rare disease discovery and diagnosis.
  • Tau Ceti (mathematics). This open, community-driven project is building a shared autoformalized library of mathematics in Lean, a language that lets computers check every proof.
  • Centre for Population Genomics. A joint initiative between Australia’s Garvan Institute of Medical Research and Murdoch Children’s Research Institute, it increases the inclusion of Australia’s multicultural communities in genomic resources and builds tools for rare disease diagnosis.

What’s next

Many of these collaborations are still in their early stages, and we’re eager to see how they can support novel research and scientific discovery. We look forward to sharing the impact of this work and showcasing new ways of working in these scientific fields.

As AI changes how science is done, our AI for Science program will continue to support and collaborate with scientists, institutions, and foundations. We hope to expand these efforts to even more partners around the world.

item.title: Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude…
item.description: Full title: Smart reports, surveys, and pooled group budgets for Claude Enterprise
item.content:encoded:
Smart reports show what that work is, and where that work is happening, in-app surveys capture their feedback about how Claude is enabling them to do new work, and pooled group budgets let admins set one shared budget per team. All three are now generally available for Claude Enterprise.

Smart reports show how your teams work in Claude, and how to spread what’s working

Smart reports surface what a team gets done with Claude, and what that work costs. The reports show ambitious work your teams are doing with Claude, and how Claude made it possible. They then show how to turn that work into repeatable workflows, so the rest of your organization can do it too.

Pick a team, a date range, and the products to include. Claude analyzes a sample of the team’s transcripts and groups the work into workstreams. See the spend for each one, the deliverables produced, and the most common points of friction, such as a missing connector or a failed tool call.

Each report has one consolidated list of recommendations, including recurring workflows to turn into skills and rules to add to your code repository. Share any finding as an artifact with the people who can act on it. Reports also answer custom questions about model usage and cost, and admins can save their questions and custom insights as templates to reuse in future reports. If a spend limit is holding someone back, admins with billing permission can raise it from the report.

Owners can let team leads who aren’t admins run reports for their own groups, so the people closest to the work act on the findings. Smart reports help admins understand adoption and inform investment planning, but they aren’t for evaluating individual performance or making employment decisions.

“We use smart reports across several initiatives. They give our applied AI team a grounded view of how Claude is being used across the company, which helps us prioritize what to do next and drive greater impact.”

Keren Koshman, Head of Applied AI

“Claude smart reports give us a new level of visibility into how AI is actually being used across our organization. What's especially valuable is the ability to turn those insights into action, helping us identify high-value use cases, shape our enablement strategy, and focus learning where it can have the greatest impact.”

Michele Bleser, VP, Business Transformation

“Each smart report is based on tens of thousands of sessions, surfacing the most common pain points and the recurring workflows worth turning into skills. It’s exactly the visibility we’ve been looking for to get more value out of Claude.”

Ran Yitzhaki, Software Engineer

“Smart reports give us greater visibility into how AI is used across the enterprise, helping inform decisions about deployment and governance. Early insights from smart reports are helping us identify effective workflows and emerging skills, providing a foundation for sharing what works more broadly across the organization.”

Vivek Kulkarni, Managing Director, AI Transformation

“I'm very close to how our teams use Claude, and smart reports still surfaced things I didn't know. That matters, because driving enablement at our scale means knowing where teams are thriving and where they need support. It's become a go-to part of my toolkit for those conversations with leaders across DoorDash.”

John Jannone, AI Enablement Lead, Engineering Enablement

“Smart reports show us how teams use Claude, from coding Docusign IAM, our AI-native contracting platform, to everyday work. That visibility helps us show leadership real outcomes, fix connector bottlenecks, and scale what's working across teams.”

Kamlesh Mallikarjunan, AI Employee Experience, Lead Product Manager

Keren Koshman, Head of Applied AI

Early insights from smart reports are helping us identify effective workflows and emerging skills, providing a foundation for sharing what works more broadly across the organization.”

Vivek Kulkarni, Managing Director, AI Transformation

“I'm very close to how our teams use Claude, and smart reports still surfaced things I didn't know. That matters, because driving enablement at our scale means knowing where teams are thriving and where they need support. It's become a go-to part of my toolkit for those conversations with leaders across DoorDash.”

John Jannone, AI Enablement Lead, Engineering Enablement

“Smart reports show us how teams use Claude, from coding Docusign IAM, our AI-native contracting platform, to everyday work. That visibility helps us show leadership real outcomes, fix connector bottlenecks, and scale what's working across teams.”

Kamlesh Mallikarjunan, AI Employee Experience, Lead Product Manager

1/6

In-app surveys capture feedback

In-app surveys add the team's own perspective on that work. The default questions focus on value: the most valuable thing someone has done with Claude recently, how Claude changed the time that work took, which use of Claude a teammate should copy, and, if the team lost access tomorrow, what would break or slow down first. Admins can customize or remove questions and choose who receives a survey, when it runs, and where it appears. Members see it as a short card after a reply in the tool they’re already working in.

Responses appear on the survey page as they arrive, and admins can export them to a spreadsheet. In-app surveys can now be enabled for organizations that use customer-managed encryption keys, and for organizations that set one retention period for all data, surveys and their responses are deleted on that schedule.

In-app surveys are treated as your data, so Anthropic accesses them only as necessary to operate the service.

Pooled group budgets put spend where the work happens

Pooled group budgets give a group one shared monthly budget, so people who use Claude heavily are less likely to hit an individual limit early in the month while others leave budget unspent. Member limits still work as a guardrail against unusually high individual use. Every request counts against both, and a member stops at whichever runs out first. When someone hits a limit, they can request more from inside Claude, and the request goes to admins for review. The setup suggests an amount based on the group's recent usage, and admins with billing permissions receive email alerts at 50%, 75%, 95%, and 100% of a budget.

Getting started

Smart reports, in-app surveys, and pooled group budgets are generally available today for Claude Enterprise. Availability varies by configuration, including for organizations with a HIPAA configuration or customer-managed encryption keys. Visit the Help Center for eligibility and detailed setup steps.

item.title: IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the c…
item.description: Full title: IDC brings Quanta into Claude and adopts Claude across the company
item.content:encoded:
IDC Research (IDC), a global leader in technology intelligence for more than 60 years, worked with Anthropic to bring IDC Quanta into Claude, available to IDC customers today. IDC Quanta gives customers access to IDC’s trusted and validated forecasts, market data, research, and more, and now, they can ask questions in Claude to get answers enriched with IDC’s insights in minutes. IDC has also rolled Claude out across the company, where teams use it every day.

Applying market research has traditionally meant reading through long reports to get to the answers a customer needs, such as a vendor shortlist or a competitive brief. Now, an IDC customer describes the market, strategy, or purchase they're working on, and the IDC Quanta MCP connector for Claude returns finished analysis built on IDC's trusted forecasts and data.

What customers can do with IDC Quanta in Claude

IDC Quanta, an AI-powered technology intelligence platform that helps customers do better work, faster, with credible, verified intelligence from IDC’s proprietary data and research. In Claude, IDC Quanta enables customers to benchmark performance, size markets, choose vendors, and shape strategy. It’s as simple as a customer describing the question they're working on, and Claude answering it using IDC's intelligence.

The questions that users ask vary by role, but they tend to look like this:

  • Competitive briefs: A corporate strategy lead asks Claude for a competitor brief. Claude returns the competitor’s positioning, market share, product capabilities, and recent acquisitions, cited to IDC's research. A job that used to take a day’s worth of research is complete in minutes.
  • Vendor shortlists: A CIO evaluating procurement software asks Claude which vendors are the best fit based on her existing architecture and unique business requirements. Claude returns the top three by IDC's procurement database and MarketScape research as an Excel scorecard, ready for the evaluation team to act on.
  • Analysis of their own numbers: A CFO uploads next year's IT budget, and asks how it compares to IDC's forecast. Claude returns where the two differ, and by how much, while updated data stays private to the customer.

IDC Quanta works wherever the customer already uses Claude, including the Claude app on desktop and mobile, Cowork, and the Microsoft Office add-ins. It gives Claude the same data and definitions an IDC analyst works from, so a market share or growth rate matches what IDC would publish, and each answer cites the IDC document or dataset it came from.

How IDC uses Claude internally

IDC has also put Claude to work across the company, where its engineers, product, marketing and sales teams are using it daily to build, plan, and sell. A clear example of the difference it's making is in engineering: IDC's engineers rebuilt the internal data repository its analysts use for research in three weeks instead of an estimated three months, and since they began using Claude Code for testing, bugs in the code they ship have come down significantly.

Engineering was the first team to adopt Claude, and the rest of the company has followed. Here's how they're using it:

  • Building and testing software: Product managers use Claude Code to build working prototypes before engineering starts, which has cut the time it takes a feature to reach engineering from months to weeks. Engineers use it to run tests in parallel, and a code review that once filled five days is done in about 30 minutes.
  • Planning and strategy: Product teams give Cowork their research and internal files, and it writes the first draft of the plan. Planning sprints that took three weeks now take three days. Writing a new test to check that code works now takes about 20 minutes, down from days.
  • Optimizing sales: IDC's sales team runs a tool built with Claude that reads an export from the company's CRM. In minutes, it tells each rep which of their deals have stalled and which are worth chasing.
  • Producing marketing content: IDC's content marketing team built an assistant in Claude to draft much of its marketing content. It optimizes the content for search and AI answer engines (SEO/AEO), and checks it against buyer personas and IDC's own research. From there, the team edits, proofs, and publishes the work, publishing content faster than it could on its own

“Assessing the impact of a competitor’s acquisition used to mean a market intelligence professional spending hours pulling multiple reports, synthesizing the findings, and turning them into an executive-ready brief. Now, they can open Claude, ask what that acquisition means for their business, and get a board-ready analysis in minutes, grounded in IDC’s research and more than 15 billion data points,” said Lorenzo Larini, CEO, IDC. “We brought IDC Quanta into Claude because that’s where many of our customers already work, giving them a faster, more intuitive way to put IDC’s trusted data and research to work.”

“IDC has spent 60 years helping leaders make better technology decisions, and now it’s using Claude to rethink how its teams work and how it delivers value to its customers,” said Paul Smith, Chief Commercial Officer, Anthropic.

Getting started

IDC Quanta customers who use Claude can add the IDC Quanta connector from within Claude. Others can contact IDC or book a demo. To learn more about Claude for Enterprise, visit anthropic.com/enterprise.
