item.title: Introducing Claude Duet
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re opening a research preview of Claude Duet, a new app where Claude works as a proactive agent. It comes to you with what needs your attention, completes tasks you ask of it, keeps working even when you step away, and checks with you before it acts on your behalf. We built Claude Duet for professionals and small business owners with more on their plates than they can track.

It’s available as a standalone app on iOS and Android, and on claude.ai. For this research preview, Claude Duet is included in Pro and Max plans and uses the same usage limits as the rest of Claude. To get access, join the waitlist (opens in new tab).

Put your attention where it matters most

We designed Claude Duet to be a partner you can trust. Professionals of all kinds have to juggle many decisions a day, and we think they’ll find Claude Duet most useful. It helps you prioritize where to spend your time and energy, and to leave room for the ambitious projects that felt impossible or daunting before.

What makes Claude Duet so helpful is its judgment. We designed it around Claude Opus 5.5 (opens in new tab) and built it to be resourceful and to decide what needs you, what can wait, and when to check with you first.

Each morning, it sends you a short brief on the most important items across your connected apps. Throughout the day, it keeps tabs on those apps and messages you only when something needs your attention. You can also hand it tasks of all shapes—from simple administrative tasks of scheduling meetings to more complex ones, such as building dashboards with dozens of tools, creating financial or sales forecasts, prototyping, and building web apps.

Safety and discretion are built in

Claude Duet draws on years of security, safety, and privacy work on agents, both our own and the infrastructure businesses use to run theirs:

  • Claude Duet draws on our framework for trustworthy agents (opens in new tab), which also guides agents like Claude Code and Claude in Chrome.
  • Claude Duet’s handling of credentials follows the design we use for Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab), so it never directly sees your passwords or sign-in tokens.
  • Actions are approved by our auto mode classifier (opens in new tab), the same safeguard that protects Claude and Claude Code from taking steps you didn’t ask for.
  • Claude Duet’s defenses against hidden instructions and prompt injection come from our browser-use research (opens in new tab), and our models and safeguards also cover this more broadly.
  • We run adversarial tests for Claude Duet’s security infrastructure. Red teams and an external firm penetration tested Claude Duet, and it’s covered by our public bug bounty program (opens in new tab).

How Duet handles sensitive information. We’re also releasing Claude Duet with a new dedicated classifier and safety system prompt that checks each message and guards against leaks of sensitive information. An agent that reads email and sends messages for you is constantly deciding where information should go. This new classifier and prompt are designed to reject requests to share the strictest tier of information, including credit card numbers and government identification. Other sensitive information, such as health or personal finances, are let through only when you’ve explicitly instructed Claude Duet to send it.

We’re continuing to develop and strengthen these protections, and will share more details about how Claude Duet is designed for safety in the coming days.

How testers are using Claude Duet

People at Anthropic have been using Claude Duet to accomplish more, but also to leave more room for thinking and being present. Boris Cherny, who leads our Claude Code team, talks through his mental to-do list with Claude Duet on walks, instead of saving the work for his desk. Chelsea Larsson, who leads our model and product behavior design team, hands Claude Duet her to-do list before leaving to be with her kids and it saves the results for an evening report. And the team behind Claude Duet uses it to build the product. Karan Ahuja, who leads the team, works with it to schedule user interviews, partner with him on prototypes, and even ship code.

We gave small business owners and entrepreneurs early access to Claude Duet, and some have been using it to help run their businesses. Here’s what some of them said:

Jess gets a rundown from Claude Duet each morning. One day, without being asked, it flagged a property showing that was on her calendar for the wrong day. “[This is] exactly the kind of thing I want caught without having to ask,” she said.

Jess Provencher, broker and owner, Pro Homes

Amin owns Shahs of Kabob in South Florida with about 110 employees. He’s used Claude Duet for accounting, customer support, and marketing, and has worked through his invoices store by store. “It brings it all together,” he said. “I don’t need to open up 100 tabs.”

Amin Ebrahimi, owner, Shahs of Kabob

Mya had a call coming up with a potential client. Claude Duet saw it on her calendar and prepared a brief. It also noticed the call fell right before her flight and offered to move it. “I didn’t realize that it was right before my flight,” she said. “I love that proactivity.”

Mya Dalton, a brand strategist

How Claude Duet works

Your context from Claude is the foundation. Claude Duet carries over your memory, skills, and connected apps from your Claude account, so setting it up requires minimal work. What changes is how you work together: Claude Duet comes to you first, and you can message it through typing or voice in one ongoing thread, so a quick reply and a weeklong project both start in the same place.

Work continues when you step away. Claude Duet has a virtual machine with its own browser, so it doesn’t require your laptop or phone to be on. Describe a task in a short message, and it works out which apps to use and what steps to take in the background. You’ll receive a notification when the task is complete or needs your review.

Receive a message when something needs you. Claude Duet checks your connected accounts every few hours, because checking nonstop would use up your plan’s limits much faster. We’re continuing to test its judgment about when to message you, and we’ll keep tuning it based on what testers tell us. You can also tell it what you want to hear about and how often.

Important decisions stay with you. Claude Duet reads, drafts, and prepares work on its own. But before it sends a message, makes a payment, signs a document, or deletes anything, it shows you exactly what it’s about to do and waits for your approval. A few things are off-limits even with your approval, like trading securities or moving money between accounts. You’re also able to disconnect any app Claude Duet has access to.

Connect with the tools your business runs on. Claude Duet can use the over 6,000 connectors and plugins in the Claude Marketplace (opens in new tab) to:

  • Find the Gmail and Slack messages you’ve missed and help you reply.
  • Check Intuit QuickBooks or Stripe for unpaid invoices and draft reminders.
  • Prepare and run payroll in Gusto, with hours, bonuses, and reimbursements filled in.
  • Draft a job posting and, once you edit and approve, post it to LinkedIn.
  • Help prepare agreements and send them for review and signature through Docusign.
  • Draft follow-up emails using the contact and deal history in HubSpot.
  • Turn your product launch into a social campaign in Canva.
  • Set up, design, and manage your Shopify store. Coming soon, a richer visual editor will let you design your storefront and preview it before anything goes live.

You can also use Claude Duet to purchase things for your business using Link, Stripe’s digital wallet. Claude Duet confirms the item with you, and Link asks you to approve the spend. It then pays with a virtual card, so your real card number isn’t shared. It can also use Shop Pay from Shopify to check out at online stores. Coming soon, with your permission, it will be able to sign in to sites with logins you’ve saved in 1Password.

Join the research preview

This is an early version of Claude Duet, and it still might misread a thread or miscalibrate what’s urgent. We built its core functionality around work, so personal errands, such as booking tickets, aren’t quite as strong, and it can’t yet show you its browser. For now, Claude Duet lives in its own app, separate from the main Claude app. What we learn from early users will shape how the two work together.

During the research preview, Claude Duet shares your plan’s usage limits with the rest of Claude, and it uses them differently than a typical conversation does. Its background checks count toward those limits, and larger tasks, like building a financial model or a deck, require more model turns and background work.

We’re starting today with Pro and Max users in the US. Join the waitlist (opens in new tab) and we’ll email as soon as Claude Duet’s ready for you.

item.title: Claude Security now scans continuously and tracks fixes
item.content:encoded:
Since Claude Security entered public beta in April, thousands of organizations have used it to find over a million vulnerabilities.

Instead of waiting for someone to start a scan, Claude Security now keeps up with your repositories as your code changes, keeps track of which findings get fixed, and uses what your team tells it about your environment to decide what matters. Claude Security is powered by our full family of models, including Claude Mythos, with no Cyber Verification Program access required.

The latest version of Claude Security is available today in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers. Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Continuous monitoring keeps up with your code

A scan captures one moment, and code changes every day. Teams told us they wanted coverage that stays current without anyone having to schedule it.

Create a project, connect your repositories through the Claude GitHub app (including GitHub Enterprise Server) or with an access token from GitLab and other Git providers, and choose the branch and scope for each. Claude runs a deep baseline scan, then scans changes regularly based upon their risk and complexity, so your list of findings stays close to the current state of your code.

A project can hold multiple repositories, so Claude can catch issues that live between services, like a backend that trusts input a client was supposed to validate.

Findings are marked fixed when the fix ships

Most fixes happen outside the tool that found the issue. Claude Security checks open findings against the code that changed and marks them fixed when the fix lands, whether your team fixed it in Claude Code or in a separate process. If Claude Security finds the issue again later, the finding reopens automatically.

Your team’s knowledge shapes the scan

Every environment has controls a scanner can’t see from the code alone. Teams wanted a way to tell Claude Security about those controls, and to look across services that depend on each other. Now, each project has a knowledge base where you can describe how your code is deployed, which security policies apply, and anything a new security engineer on your team would need to know.

Claude Security also generates a threat model from your code that your team can review and edit. Subsequent scans use those threat models to decide what’s worth flagging. Added context also helps Claude Security skip risks your environment already handles.

Severity and exploit paths for every finding

Each finding comes with a severity rating, judged against your project’s threat model, and an explanation of how an attacker could reach the vulnerable code, so teams can fix what’s actually reachable first. Findings can include a diagram of the attack path.

Findings reach your tools, with controls for larger rollouts

The new API lets you integrate Claude Security into your existing workflows. You can list and read projects and findings, resolve or reopen findings, and create and manage projects and their repositories. Users can create a personal access token in Claude Security settings, and it can only see and change what the user can. Webhooks can also notify your systems when a new finding lands.

Claude Security is also available as an MCP connector in Claude.ai and Claude Code. An engineer can pull up a finding, ask Claude about it, start the fix, and mark it resolved in the same session.

New role-based access controls let admins decide who can view projects, triage findings, and create projects. Organizations can open Claude Security to more teams that own the code without giving everyone access to create projects.

Getting started

The latest version of Claude Security is available in public beta for Claude Enterprise customers starting today. Admins can enable it in the admin console and set who on their team can access it.

Use the Getting Started Guide to set up your first project, and visit the Help Center for more details.

Organizations receive $25,000 in free usage credits each month, for two months. The offer applies to usage through December 31, 2026. You can view full terms in the Help Center.

Jon Donovan, Software Engineer, IonQ

Jake Meredith, Product Security, Gusto

Joe Coniglio, Security Engineer, IonQ

item.title: Investing in the public benefit
item.content:encoded:
Today, we’re committing a portion of Anthropic’s shares to the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund, a new entity with a structure that increases the stake as the company grows. Subject to stockholder approval, 5% of Anthropic’s shares will be committed today, with an additional 2% added at the board’s discretion for every 50% increase in the company’s value above a set baseline.

As a public benefit corporation, most of our work in pursuit of our mission takes place inside the company: research relevant to AI safety and interpretability; applied biomedical research; discounts on Claude for nonprofits and scientific institutions. These activities have both a public benefit component and for-profit value, so we house them directly in the company.

The Anthropic Public Benefit Fund will have increased flexibility and scale, enabling us to pursue our mission in new ways: for example, we might explore large donations to traditional nonprofits or direct distributions to specific populations.

One example is labor market impacts. AI may generate enormous economic value, but it could also cause instability for many workers. Anthropic has already committed $200 million to studying and addressing this issue, but given the pace of AI progress, bolder approaches may be needed. The Fund will have the versatility to pursue them.

We’re establishing the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund as a wholly-owned LLC—rather than a 501(c)(3) or other format—to give adjustability between different forms of giving. None of the Anthropic equity held by the LLC will be used for lobbying or political giving, in the US or abroad.

Because of the way the Fund is structured, the more Anthropic grows, the larger the share of the company that can be dedicated expressly to the public good. It is common practice for tech companies to offer escalating compensation awards to their executives. We are instead directing that equity to the public benefit.

This builds on commitments our co-founders and employees have already made. When Anthropic was founded, our co-founders pledged to donate 80% of their equity holdings, and since founding we have also operated an equity donation match program that allows employees to pledge equity which Anthropic matches. Approximately half of our employees participate in this program. When combined with today’s announcement, roughly 20% of Anthropic shares will be dedicated to the public good, plus any additional percentage that could be added if the company reaches specific valuation milestones.

In the coming months, we will share more about the Anthropic Public Benefit Fund’s structure and governance, including the valuation milestones that may add to its stake. We will also report on our progress to date against our mission in an upcoming public benefit report.

item.title: How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Manag…
item.description: Full title: How an Anthropic BDR in Japan runs his day with Claude Managed Agents
item.content:encoded:
As a business development representative on Anthropic's Japan team, my job is to show Japanese companies how Claude can simplify and automate their workflows, but until earlier this year, most of mine were still manual. I was spending a couple of hours each morning routing and qualifying leads, then writing emails in Japanese or English. In the time I had left, I was updating our CRM, often a day or more behind. Now my agents prepare most of that before my day starts, and I review it.

The first Claude-run workflow I built was pretty scrappy, but it did the job. I'd hand Claude one piece of my work at a time, correct what it got wrong, and save those corrections. Over time, that grew into a handful of agents, each covering a different routine.

Word got around quickly, and teammates started asking for my prompts and skills so they could build their own. All I could send them was a zip file with my skills and a few Markdown files from the knowledge base, which they had to upload to Claude and then answer a round of setup questions before anything worked. My own setup was getting harder to keep track of, too. Each agent was a skill, a scheduled task and a shared folder, and I changed them by asking Claude in whatever chat I had open, so the same skill was being edited from lots of different conversations.

I wanted to define each agent once, in one place, and be able to see every change I'd made to it. So I decided to try Claude Managed Agents (opens in new tab) (beta), our managed agent infrastructure on the Claude Platform.

I was hesitant to try it at first. The docs talk about schedules, tools, and credential vaults, and I'm a sales rep, so I assumed Managed Agents was for developers who can build and maintain the necessary infrastructure. I tried it anyway because my agents already existed, and I only had to move them over.

It turned out I didn't need to be a developer. I described each agent's job in plain language, Claude wrote a few short setup scripts, and I ran them from the terminal on my laptop. (If you're starting from scratch, the Console also has a quickstart with ready-made agent templates.) Since then, there has been no infrastructure for me to look after.

In this post, I'll walk through how I designed and prototyped the fleet, why I moved it to Managed Agents, how Claude Tag picks up anything that falls outside the routine, how it all changed my week, and what I'd tell sellers who want to build their own agents to automate manual, repetitive workflows.

Designing my fleet of agents

I divided up my workflow across several agents and gave every agent one clear job. A single responsibility keeps each one easy to reason about and easy to track, especially when something is off. I also gave every agent a Japanese name, because they mostly work in Japanese. Together they're called the Nakama, "the crew," or more literally, the companions you work with:

  • Furiwake ("sorting") kicks off first: it reads the daily inbound queue and routes each lead to the right rep on the team, balancing the number of leads and the priority of each one and checking who's in that day, so every lead has an owner before any of us start our day. At the end of each run it posts a report to a dedicated Slack channel (every lead in, every lead assigned) so I can track the handoff.
  • ***Sabaki* **("handling") triages the leads that are assigned to me: it qualifies each lead, categorizes it against pre-set criteria, takes the defined next step for that category (draft a reply pointing them to to self-serve, craft a customized first email), updates the lead record in Salesforce, and drafts the first-touch email. It sources the draft's contents from the Nakama's shared knowledge base, a memory store (opens in new tab) every agent reads and writes (more on this below).
  • ***Henji* **("reply") scans my inbox hourly for customer emails that need a response and prepares a draft reply in Japanese or English, depending on the thread, drawing on the same knowledge base as Sabaki. I can review, edit, and send the draft.
  • Shoudan ("opportunity") reads recent customer interactions and pushes updates into Salesforce, so opportunity records stay current without manual data entry.
  • ***Nokori* **("what remains") runs at the end of the day: it scans my calendar, reads the attached meeting transcripts, summarizes each meeting, and drafts the follow-ups, again from the same knowledge base.

Each agent runs on a schedule. A sixth agent, the Nakama's coordinator, is the fleet’s operations manager. It updates the agents’ instructions and the shared knowledge base between runs. When I want to change how an agent works, I write what I want in plain language in the Nakama’s Slack channel. Only I can post requests for changes to agents’ instructions and system prompts. The coordinator checks that channel every 15 minutes or so, picks up the request, and makes the update.

Prototyping the fleet in Claude

You don't need Managed Agents to start. I prototyped the whole fleet in Claude first, using the following pieces:

  • A skill per agent: the instructions for one job.
  • A scheduled task for each skill, so I don’t need to run it manually.
  • A shared folder on my laptop as the knowledge base every skill writes its learnings back into: the difference between what it drafted and what I sent, plus anything new it dug up along the way.

On Managed Agents, the skill became the agent's system prompt, the scheduled task became a schedule on the agent's deployment (opens in new tab), and the shared folder became a memory store. I still ask for changes in plain language, but now I do it all in one Slack channel, and each change to an agent's instructions is saved as a new version, so each agent keeps a numbered history of its instructions. I'd suggest starting in Claude and moving your agents to Managed Agents once you have more than you can comfortably keep track of.

Running the fleet on Claude Managed Agents

Three things I got on Managed Agents that mattered most for my workflow:

The agents can run in the background

The agents run on their schedule whether my laptop is open or not, even when it's offline. The schedule is part of each agent's deployment. I could schedule skills in Claude too, but each of those schedules was a task set up in my own app. On Managed Agents, I set the cadence and timezone in the Console, next to the deployed agent's instructions and tools, and I have no cron jobs to maintain on the side. If a run goes wrong, I can open it in the Console and see each step the agent took. And while I'm trying out a change to an agent, the scheduled runs keep using the version that’s deployed, so a half-finished edit doesn't end up in tomorrow's run.

The Nakama shares one memory and learns from my edits

Every agent reads and writes the same memory store (opens in new tab), so any agent can use the others’ learnings. The agents compare the drafts they wrote with the emails I sent, and they save each difference as a note on how I'd phrase it. They also keep whatever new information they dig up while researching an answer, from our internal docs and our official websites. I fix a phrasing once in Henji's drafts, and Sabaki and Nokori stop making the same mistake.

Credentials live in a managed vault with scoped permissions

My agents have access to my email and our Salesforce records, but since these are customer conversations and company records, I wanted that access under control. The credentials live in managed vaults (opens in new tab), which protect credentials agents use to log in to outside services, such as OAuth access and refresh tokens, API keys, and personal access tokens. Each agent’s deployment uses only the vaults its job needs, it never sees the credentials, and I can revoke access in one step.

Handing the next steps to Claude Tag

For most of what the Nakama produces, I only need to read a draft in my inbox and send it, or glance at an updated Salesforce record. But some items need a follow-up step, such as figuring out an upgrade path or a purchasing route, or escalating an issue to another team.

For those, the agents don't stop and wait for me. They hand the item to Claude Tag (opens in new tab) (in beta). Claude Tag is Claude set up as a member of our Slack workspace: anyone in a channel it has joined, a person or one of my agents, can tag @Claude with a request and it picks the request up and works on it in the thread. Once it's configured in your workspace there is nothing new to learn. You tag Claude the way you would a colleague.

In my setup it works like this. An agent posts the action item to the Nakama's Slack channel and tags Claude. Claude reads the thread, checks our rules and the terms that apply, lays out the options, and drafts what's needed. It tags me when a step needs my review or sign-off. When a customer or another team needs to reply first, Claude sets a reminder for itself to check back on a set day. In the thread below, it set a reminder for Tuesday to check whether the customer had replied and whether the deal desk had answered the ticket. When the reminder comes due, Claude checks both and posts where things stand in the same thread. If someone needs a nudge, it drafts the message and tags me to send it.

Claude also posts a morning brief of product and pricing updates. The Nakama coordinator picks up that brief and writes the necessary changes into the shared knowledge base.

What changed in my week

Now that Claude prepares inbound replies and keeps CRM records current (mostly) without my manual input, my role is to review anything that requires human judgment. A written rulebook defines each agent's lane and items like pricing questions, sensitive accounts, or ambiguous asks route to me. Every email draft from Henji, Sabaki, or Nokori arrives with a short summary at the top of what's going on, so I don't have to trace the whole thread to understand the context: I read the summary, confirm, make revisions, and send.

Looking at the weekly log of what the Nakama gets through and counting each task as the time it would have taken me to do manually, the fleet saves me around 60 hours of work. I spend the time that frees up on work that agents can't effectively do (yet): conversations with customers, outbound strategy, cross-functional projects, and helping teammates build their own fleets.

Designing agents to be more efficient

Scheduled agents run every day whether I'm watching or not, so waste can add up, in cost and reliability. Some of the most common mistakes include adding to existing instructions rather than updating them, giving agents more context than they need for their tasks, and running every job on the biggest model at the highest effort level.

Most of what keeps the agents efficient is how I designed the fleet: each agent has one job, so its instructions stay focused on that job; each working agent runs on a schedule, so it wakes up, does its pass, and stops; and the agents share memory, so a correction made once is reused everywhere.

The other big factor is which model each agent runs on. Once an agent's job is well defined, it may not need our most capable model. Furiwake and Shoudan follow a written rulebook, so they run on Sonnet, our smaller model. Sabaki, Nokori and the coordinator run on Opus, our larger model, because their work needs more judgment. The coordinator needs it most, since it edits the other agents' instructions and one bad edit would reach every agent. Henji needs as much judgment as Sabaki, because every customer's email is different, but it also runs more often than any other agent, all through the working day. Running it on Opus every time would be the most expensive option, so I use the advisor strategy (opens in new tab) in Managed Agents: Henji runs on Sonnet, and when it reaches a decision it can't make on its own, it asks Opus for advice. The advisor reads what Henji has done so far and sends back a plan, a correction, or a stop signal, and Henji then finishes the draft for my review. I also set each agent's effort level (how long the model thinks before it answers) separately from its model, and I raise it only where the reasoning is hard, as with Henji's replies.

What I learned

Three things I'd pass on to anyone building their own fleet.

  • You don't need a detailed prompt every time. Describe the job once, let Claude draft, fix the draft, and let it keep the fix.
  • The knowledge base matters more than the prompt. Every correction and past interaction is saved where all the agents can read it and write to it, so Claude takes its context from there instead of from a longer prompt. It took a few hundred cheap rounds of drafting, fixing, and saving to get the drafts to sound like me.
  • Give Claude more room, sooner. At first I kept doing the tasks that I assumed needed me: updating the knowledge base, or editing each agent's instructions by hand. Both worked fine once I let go of them. The agents now write what they learn into the knowledge base themselves, and the coordinator updates the other agents' instructions when I ask in plain English. I had been too cautious with work I could trust the agents to do.

item.title: An update on independent evaluators
item.content:encoded:
Last month, we committed to stronger independent, third-party assessment of our models and safety practices. We also signed the White House Accord on Super Intelligence, in which companies pledged to partner with independent external auditors or evaluators. Today, we’re announcing that we’ve started to give employee-like access to a team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models.

METR will publish the results of its risk assessments. Over the past year, we’ve worked with METR on several reviews of our Risk Reports. We’re also working with SecureBio and Accenture as evaluators, and are in early discussions with several other organizations, including Hugging Face.

Here, we explain our approach to working with evaluators.

Why we work with independent evaluators

As models have become more powerful, they’ve required stronger safeguards and more challenging risk assessments. We want to be publicly accountable for the decisions we’re making. But we can’t publicly share all the information relevant to our safety work. Some of it could be useful to malicious actors, or is commercially sensitive, like compute or training information. Instead, we’re giving third-party evaluators deep access to our information, and are having them share evidence and reasoned conclusions about the risks involved in building our models. We aim to close the gap between what evaluators understand about a frontier AI company’s systems and what the company itself understands.

To evaluate frontier models, evaluators need the following:

  • Expertise in assessing the capabilities of frontier models, including understanding the way evaluations can go wrong, such as alignment faking.
  • Independence: they shouldn’t hold equity in the company they’re evaluating, or be financially or operationally dependent on it.
  • Enough access to meaningfully evaluate risks. Beyond access to the latest models, evaluators also need visibility into how those models were trained, into how our safeguards function, and more.
  • Freedom to publish observations and assessments of a model or a process.

Although the analogy isn’t exact, bank supervision operates on similar logic. Banks know more about their own risk positions than outsiders do, so regulators assign resident examiners to work inside the largest banks. If a bank’s risk-taking could threaten the public, third parties try to see that in advance.

For the AI industry, this is a step toward robust safety oversight. We’re moving quickly with multiple evaluators and learning actively about what kinds of partnership work. We’re committed to sharing updates as we go.

What we mean by “employee-like access”

We’ve onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space, and access to internal tools and systems that are roughly on par with what our own risk assessment teams have access to. Outside a small number of clearly defined categories (e.g., data about customers, attorney-client privileged information, or information about our model architectures), Anthropic employees are encouraged to share information with them just as they would with a fellow employee working on alignment risk.1

METR will publish its analysis of our risk levels, incidents, or practices. Anthropic can’t veto publication, but we can require them to redact information if it falls into predefined categories such as reproducing confidential IP. (Anthropic ultimately decides what information does and does not fall into these categories, although METR reserves the right to make certain statements about the level of access and information it received.)2

Our engagement with METR is limited to a small team operating under enforceable agreements. Other METR employees are siloed from that team’s work, including researchers who work with us on other projects. Embedded evaluation gives a few qualified people working under Anthropic’s security standards a close view of how we operate. It’s not a way for other organizations to obtain our information, or that of our customers and partners.

Our other evaluator partnerships

We’re working on several other partnerships. Because these other partnerships are still in early stages, we’re providing these evaluators with more limited information, and they have more limited publication rights. Our goal with these early engagements is to make sure that our partners protect confidential information and have the requisite resources and expertise to evaluate our models. As partnerships progress and we build trust, we hope to fully embed more independent evaluators.

We’re developing three tiers of access for evaluators. Over time, we hope to have several evaluators at the third tier, with each team publishing their own analysis of our risk posture and key decisions.

In the first tier, evaluators conduct narrowly scoped risk investigations. We decide what access to provide a first-tier evaluator, and evaluators can publish their findings with our approval.

In the second tier, evaluators can publish without our approval, and they have access to more information. We can still require removal of specific categories of information, though evaluators can publish their views on whether our redactions were justified.

The third tier is the arrangement we’ve described with METR, with employee-like access and publication rights similar to those of the second tier.

SecureBio is in the process of reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of our August Risk Report, after completing and publishing a pilot review of our previous risk report. After this review is complete, we will consider moving to projects with increased access.3

With Accenture and Faculty, we're working toward an ambitious partnership that includes evaluating and red-teaming models, conducting alignment assessments, testing model safeguards, and building capabilities across our organizations.

We’re embedding evaluators voluntarily, and we believe every frontier AI company should do the same.

Footnotes

01Because these evaluators (like bank examiners) may also work with other companies, we exercise caution around the possibility of inadvertent leaks. Information about architectures presents a high risk of inadvertent leaks, and its relevance to risk assessment is typically low. When it is highly relevant, we will generally seek to share it, though this will require explicit internal approvals.

02Updated on October 16 to clarify METR's current project terms with Anthropic.

03Updated on October 15 to clarify SecureBio's current project terms with Anthropic.

item.title: Code Review is now generally available
item.content:encoded:
Code Review is out of research preview and available to Claude Team and Enterprise organizations.

Eligible Claude Enterprise organizations can claim at least $10,000 in Code Review credits by January 15, 2027. Credits expire 30 days after you claim them. Terms apply.

What's new in Code Review

Coding agents keep increasing the pace at which teams write code, and the review bottleneck hasn't eased. For general availability, we made Code Review faster, better at finding the bugs that matter, and easier to tune to each of your repositories.

Since we released the research preview, Code Review has gotten sharper, catching more of the bugs that would otherwise reach production. We also run Code Review on pull requests at Anthropic, which shows us where reviews slow our own engineers down. Teams using Code Review during the preview told us the rest: it was catching real issues before a human reviewer looked at the PR, but they wanted reviews that were quieter, sized to each change, and faster. Here’s what we shipped:

  • Speed: Most reviews now finish about 3x faster (~20 minutes down to 6-10 minutes) compared to during preview.
  • Quality: Find more of the bugs that matter, with clear, concise findings that state the problem, what triggers it, and the fix in a few sentences.
  • Flexibility: Admins choose Quick, Standard or Deep for each repository, so routine codebases get a quick pass and the most critical ones get a deep review. Every level delivers high-quality reviews.

Get started

Code Review is now generally available for Team and Enterprise plans.

  • For admins: Enable Code Review in your Claude Code settings, install the GitHub App, and select repositories you’d like to run reviews on.
  • For developers: Once enabled, reviews run automatically on new PRs. No configuration needed.

Explore the docs for more information.

item.title: Preparing for the 2026 US midterms
item.content:encoded:
Earlier this year, we shared an update on our election safeguards, which described how we measure and prevent political bias, detect misuse, and direct people to accurate voting information.

Below, we outline how we've built on that work and continued to strengthen our election safeguards ahead of this year’s US midterms.

How people use Claude for elections and politics

Our goal is for Claude to be a useful tool for political conversations, while preventing election-related abuse. That starts with understanding how people actually use Claude in these contexts. To do this, we used Anthropic Insights to develop a new analysis of 250,000 conversations over the course of a recent one-week period.1

Today, conversations that touch broadly on politics, public policy, or social issues account for about 5.75% of all conversations in the United States on Claude.ai, our consumer app. This includes people turning to Claude to follow the news, conduct academic or professional research on public policy, learn about candidates, and navigate government services. About 0.51% of all conversations are specifically about elections or voting. As we get closer to Election Day, we expect the share of political and election-related queries to increase.

This sample suggests people rarely ask Claude whom or what to vote for. These kinds of requests showed up in about 0.01% of US Claude conversations. More often, we observed people asking Claude questions that could help them reach their own conclusions, like where candidates stand on a particular issue. Requests that violated our election integrity policies were even less common, appearing in about 0.002% of conversations.2

How many US Claude.ai conversations touch on politics, are about elections, or ask Claude whom or what to vote for. Each dot represents 1 in every 10,000 conversations in a random sample of about 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026, which Claude classified using a privacy-preserving method. Because requests for a recommendation on whom or what to vote for are so rare, we show the upper end of a 95% confidence interval for that group. Examples are illustrative only. Most of the requests we see are informational in nature. People turn to Claude to make sense of geopolitical events, research candidates, draft documents, assist with coursework, and weigh arguments for and against policies.

What people ask Claude for in political conversations. Conversations were clustered in a privacy-preserving, bottom-up manner through Anthropic Insights.

Connecting people to trusted sources

Ahead of Election Day, we've added two ways for people to get reliable information directly in their conversations with Claude. As we shared in April, when people ask Claude.ai about voter registration, polling places, or election dates, we’ll continue to display a banner linking to TurboVote, a nonpartisan resource from Democracy Works.

Later this month, Claude will start drawing official voting information from Democracy Works into its responses on Claude.ai for users in the US. Someone asking where to vote or what ID to bring to their polling place will now get an answer specific to their state, without leaving the conversation. These responses draw on publicly available information that Democracy Works collects from state and local election sources.

Official voting information presented by Democracy Works.

Additionally, Claude will begin showing up-to-date results on election night and in the days that follow, so that when people ask for current vote counts or election results, they'll be shown the latest official numbers directly in their conversation.

Measuring and preventing political bias

When people ask Claude about politics, they should get accurate and evenhanded answers that don't favor any particular political viewpoint. That’s why we test our models extensively for political bias before every model launch. Claude Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5 are our most evenhanded to date, scoring 99% on our political evenhandedness evaluation. Our latest models also engage more readily with political discussions and decline fewer requests, so people can get the information they came for. We're continuing to refine these evaluations, and also looking beyond them for new ways to pressure-test how our models handle political topics.

As part of that effort, we asked three independent groups to review how Claude handles free expression, each from a different angle with different methodologies. The Future of Free Speech, an independent think tank at Vanderbilt University, tested Claude on hundreds of requests on contentious topics, and the Foundation for American Innovation compared how Claude responded to matched prompts from the left and right, ranging from mainstream policy debates to more extreme scenarios. On both of these evaluations, most of the responses were rated as strong, engaging substantively with requests. The Collective Intelligence Project surveyed more than 2,000 people in the US, UK, and India in developing an evaluation. Through a three-stage process, participants proposed principles for handling sensitive topics, ranging from health to politics, identified topics to test, and helped develop criteria for judging model responses. CIP synthesized this input and tested for agreement across demographic and cultural groups to establish shared principles.

These evaluations also identified areas where Claude still falls short. The Future of Free Speech and the Collective Intelligence Project both found that Claude rarely refused requests, but sometimes added unsolicited caveats and counterarguments, such as inserting an opposing view into an advocacy email. And the Foundation for American Innovation found that Claude Sonnet 4.5 didn’t always hedge evenly, and was more likely to soften arguments for right-leaning positions.

We're addressing this in a few ways. We've improved how Claude responds to direct yes-or-no questions and requests for shorter answers, where we found its answers could be less balanced. We're also using these findings to improve when and how Claude adds caveats or counterarguments, so it treats requests from across the political spectrum more consistently. And we're continuing to improve how we test for uneven hedging, building on existing evaluations that use matched prompts from the left and right. More broadly, we're working to expand our political bias evaluations to better reflect real conversations and to cover candidates and voting questions as well as policy issues.

How we define misuse

Our Usage Policy prohibits using Claude to deceive voters or disrupt elections, from spreading false information about candidates or how to vote, to impersonating election officials or trying to suppress turnout. Each year, we update the policy to reflect our models’ evolving capabilities and feedback from our customers. This year’s update, which we announced last week, clarifies what our election rules cover and what they don't, and adds new examples to help people understand where the lines fall.

We know many political campaigns use Claude for legitimate, everyday tasks, so we recently published a guide to help them understand where these policies apply. It covers the many ways campaigns can put Claude to work, such as drafting press statements and fundraising emails, prepping for debates, analyzing turnout data, and building voter outreach materials. It also spells out what’s prohibited, such as using Claude to create fake social media profiles that pose as real people, mass-producing comments to inflate a campaign’s engagement, or writing content for news sites and pages that falsely claim to be independent.

Testing and strengthening our defenses

We deploy automated classifiers that are trained to detect election-related abuse. To see how these safeguards hold up in practice, we partnered with the Institute for Strategic Dialogue (ISD) and the McCain Institute, both independent research organizations, to pressure-test our protections in the US, Israel, and Brazil. Analysts tested whether Claude would assist with deceptive campaigning, misinformation, and other forms of election abuse. They began with direct requests, then broke full campaigns into smaller tasks that could look harmless on their own, such as audience research, building news sites, drafting content, and planning its distribution. They found that Claude reliably refused a single harmful request, but could miss a malicious campaign when it was spread across many individual requests that looked harmless on their own.

Building on these findings and our own, we've added new classifiers to better identify novel and multi-step misuse, including attempts to build fake social media accounts and news sites aimed at political discussions, or to run financially motivated election schemes. We also enhanced our ability to detect election-related misuse by foreign state actors, and strengthened our cyber protections for election infrastructure and campaigns. Finally, we built targeted safeguards for localized risks identified in the US, Israel, and Brazil, which all have major national elections this year.

Our threat intelligence and enforcement teams review flagged activity and take action when they confirm a violation, including banning accounts. We also routinely share examples of unintended model actions or behavior we've observed during our evaluations and internal use of Claude.

What we've found

Our recent threat intelligence report reflects a broader shift in election-related abuse trends. Political, state-aligned, and commercial actors are now incorporating AI into nearly every aspect of their influence operations, from planning and content creation to building platforms used to disseminate a message. Because we see these early stages of an operation happening on Claude, we often have a chance to stop these efforts before they ever reach the public.

Our teams have continued to investigate and prevent coordinated abuse around elections, including the US midterms. In one case, foreign-based operators of a fake news site used Claude to produce US midterm coverage favoring Russian, Iranian, and North Korean narratives. We've also observed threat actors seeking to exploit the election for financial gain, using Claude to produce fabricated news and other content designed to attract American audiences and generate advertising revenue. We banned the accounts involved in these cases and improved our ability to detect this type of abuse.

Looking ahead

More people are turning to Claude for information about this year’s elections than ever before. We have a responsibility to make sure the answers they get are accurate and balanced, and that Claude isn’t used to undermine the democratic process. We’ll continue to invest in making Claude more evenhanded, preventing and addressing misuse, and being transparent in our actions. This work will be critical in the upcoming US midterms and extends to elections around the world as well. In the coming months, we also hope to share a more comprehensive look at how people used Claude throughout the election cycle, with the goal of strengthening our election-related evaluations and safeguards.

Footnotes

01We took a random sample of 250,000 US Claude.ai consumer conversations from September 21 to 27, 2026 and analyzed them in a privacy-preserving way.

02This figure was generated from a separate analysis of 250,000 Claude.ai conversations, which were reviewed against our election integrity policy.

item.title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Gove…
item.description: Full title: Anthropic opens Singapore office and signs MOU with the Government of Singapore
item.content:encoded:
Today, we are expanding our Asia-Pacific operations by opening a new office in Singapore—our fifth in the region—and signing a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the Singapore Ministry of Digital Development and Information. Singapore is one of our most active markets anywhere in the world, and Claude is already powering Singaporean business and government services used by millions of people every day, like GovTech Singapore, Grab, and DBS. Our growing local team will ensure these organizations and many more stay on the frontier with safe, capable AI.

“We’re committed to Singapore for the long term,” said Dale Finlay, General Manager of ASEAN at Anthropic. “Our customers here hold AI to an extremely high standard, especially when it comes to reliability and security. Having a team on the ground means we can get even closer to the organizations putting Claude to work on their hardest problems.”

Supporting responsible AI in Singapore

Kai Fong Chng, Permanent Secretary of the Ministry of Digital Development and Information, and Anthropic co-founder Ben Mann signed the MOU on the sidelines of Singapore International Cyber Week. Minister for Digital Development and Information Josephine Teo and Michael Sellitto, Anthropic Head of APAC Policy, witnessed the signing. It sets out areas of cooperation in AI safety, security, and model evaluation; research on AI adoption and its impact; and responsible adoption across the public and private sectors.

“Singapore has been a leader in responsible AI, with a long track record of investment in model testing and evaluation,” said Mann. “We founded Anthropic on the belief that capability and safety have to go hand in hand. With this MOU, we’ll partner with Singapore to help ensure the transition to powerful AI goes well here, across Asia-Pacific, and around the world.”

“Singapore’s approach to AI has always been to enable innovation while keeping pace with its evolving risks. Trust is critical for businesses, workers, and the public to use AI with confidence,” said Chng. “This partnership with Anthropic reflects the Government’s commitment to scaling up the responsible adoption of AI, deepening capabilities in our companies and government agencies, and delivering impact for Singapore.”

Our work with Singapore goes back to 2023, when we joined the Generative AI Evaluation Sandbox run by the Infocomm Media Development Authority and the AI Verify Foundation. We later partnered with them on a red-teaming project in English, Mandarin, Malay, and Tamil.

Under the MOU, we plan to hold technical exchanges with Singapore’s AI safety, security, and assurance institutions on model evaluation, testing standards, and incident response. We do similar work with safety institutes around the world, where sharing technical information provides governments with a clearer view of frontier AI capabilities and risks, while helping developers build safer models.

We’ll also look for ways to strengthen AI skills in Singapore, help small and medium-sized businesses adopt AI responsibly, and support the government’s goal of building AI capability among public officers. We plan to share research and data with the government, including from the Anthropic Economic Index, and to offer technical and policy expertise as Singapore develops its rules for AI.

How Singapore is working with Claude

In our latest Economic Index, Singapore ranks second of 121 countries in Claude.ai usage relative to its population, at nearly six times what its size alone would predict.

In the public sector, more than 1,500 engineers and technical staff at the Government Technology Agency of Singapore (GovTech Singapore) have adopted Claude Code to modernize government systems and speed up software delivery. This has helped GovTech Singapore teams build, maintain, and enhance digital services more efficiently at national scale. The Cyber Security Agency of Singapore is exploring how Claude could help strengthen the country’s cyber defense.

In financial services, DBS, Southeast Asia’s largest bank, works with Claude across a range of use cases in its Singapore operations—including software development and day-to-day productivity—as part of its broader AI innovation efforts. These applications operate within the bank’s strict security and governance framework. GIC, Singapore’s sovereign wealth fund, is rolling out Claude across its investment and corporate services teams. Organizations in regulated sectors like financial services can now run Claude with in-region inference on Amazon Bedrock, helping them meet strict data processing requirements.

Singapore’s largest technology companies and startups are building with Claude too. Grab powers BriX, its sales assistant, with Claude. The assistant saves Grab’s sales teams approximately 40,000 hours every quarter and surfaces new sales opportunities. Sea—the business behind Shopee, Garena, and Monee—works with Claude to help Shopee’s customer service chatbot respond faster and more accurately, and thousands of its employees write and debug code with Claude. And Supabase—the developer platform with strong roots in Singapore—is building with Claude Code.

Building with the developer community

This week, senior leaders from Anthropic are in Singapore to open the office and meet with customers, developers, and policymakers.

Today, we hosted Builder Summit Singapore, bringing more than 300 developers together with engineering and product leaders from Anthropic. Earlier in the week, Singapore’s Claude community ambassadors held a meetup for more than 700 local builders.

Our Singapore office is now open and hiring. To learn more about joining the team, visit our careers page.

item.title: Agent observability on the Claude Platform
item.content:encoded:
You can now send OpenTelemetry (OTel) traces from Claude Managed Agents, the Messages API, and Claude SDKs to any OTel tool, and follow each step your agents take. If you already send Claude Code or Cowork traces to your observability tool, the agents you build on the Claude Platform can also show up in the same place.

Trace agents with OpenTelemetry

Trusting an agent with more access starts with tracing its model calls, tool use, and MCP server calls. Review its traces, then widen its access as it proves reliable.

Add a destination in the Claude Console, and every agent turn, model call, and tool use arrives in your observability tool as a standard OpenTelemetry trace, with latency, tokens, and IDs.

Works with your observability tools

Claude traces follow the OpenTelemetry GenAI semantic conventions, so data from Claude and other providers works in the same tools and dashboards.

  • Debug agents next to the rest of your stack. In Grafana Cloud, Honeycomb, Sentry, and Splunk, agent traces sit beside your logs and metrics, so you can see which service a slow or failed step came from.
  • Improve agents with production data. With Arize AI, Braintrust, Datadog, Langfuse, LangSmith by LangChain, New Relic, and PostHog, you can turn real traces into evals, catch quality issues, and measure whether a change helped.
  • Track usage across your organization. Send traces to Databricks Unity Gateway so platform and security teams can see token usage by team and flag unusual activity.

Claude traces also work with any other OpenTelemetry tool that accepts a standard OTLP endpoint.

Get started

OpenTelemetry traces on the Claude Platform is available in public beta. Managed Agents and the Messages API need a destination in the Claude Console, while Claude SDKs export traces automatically.

See the docs to get started.

“At Foxglove, we’re building agents that help robotics teams debug their robots. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform lets us analyze agent interactions in PostHog alongside product usage data. That helps us evaluate how our agents perform in practice, identify where they fall short, and prioritize improvements for robotics teams.”

Roman Shtylman, Co-Founder and CTO

“Claude powers some of Ramp’s most capable internal and customer-facing agents. We built Reflect, an agentic system that scores their Langfuse traces, finds recurring failures, and proposes fixes. On some agents, we’ve already cut token usage by 10–20% and made sessions 30% faster. But Reflect can only improve what it observes. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude API can feed high-fidelity instrumentation directly into that improvement loop, with no extra steps.”

David Traina, Senior Software Engineer

“At Sterling Labs, we tune our systems like a race team tunes its engine. For agents analyzing live markets 24/7, Langfuse is our pit wall. Native OpenTelemetry export from the Claude Platform streams every trace straight in with no custom instrumentation, so my team can focus on the edge, not the wiring.”

Hyon Lee, CTO

“Agents that touch a company’s books have to show their work, the same way an accountant does. Our agents run on the Claude Platform and our telemetry lives in Grafana Cloud, and native OpenTelemetry export from Claude puts each model call in the same trace as the reconciliation or journal-entry workflow it ran inside. We see the prompt version, tool calls, latency, and token spend alongside the rest of our stack, so when an auditor asks what an agent did and why, we can answer from one timeline.”

Ankush Sharma, Head of Infrastructure

item.title: Uber's CISO on building an insider threat program for AI
item.content:encoded:
Uber runs one of the world's largest real-time marketplaces, with over 40 million trips and delivery orders a day. Philip Martin, Uber's Chief Information Security Officer (CISO), leads the team that protects Uber's data and the riders, drivers, and couriers who use the platform in the real world. His team started working with Claude on threat modeling before Claude Code existed, assembling context by hand. Now, with Claude Fable, Claude gathers that context itself from code, design docs, and ticket history.

Martin thinks AI agents need the same kind of insider threat program companies already run for their employees. We spoke with him about that idea, why he thinks so much about accidental misuse, and how Uber's open-source monitoring tools work alongside Enterprise Frontier Safeguards.

How are frontier models changing your security team’s work?

The really big difference between prior models and today’s frontier models is their ability to incorporate additional context over long time horizons, and as a result, generate really specific outputs. When we're doing security reviews or threat modeling for a given service application, we can let the models consume a lot more context about the service, whether that's the code itself, design documents, issues in Jira, or historical context on what the service is supposed to do and what it interacts with.

I see the same thing emerging with teams of agents. I can imagine a world in the not-too-distant future where each service has an agent associated with it that understands that service very well, and those agents can talk to each other, the same way the services might in production, about the threat model: this is my threat model, this is where my data comes from. That team-of-agents effect will take us to the next level of efficacy.

Uber worked with our team Enterprise Frontier Safeguards. Why was this important for Uber?

One thing Anthropic and Uber have in common is a bone-deep focus on safety, albeit in very different contexts. When Uber thinks about safety, we think about rider safety, protecting personal data. Anthropic wants to prevent the misuse of its frontier models, but Uber needs to protect our customer data, our trade secrets, and any other proprietary information. Enterprise Frontier Safeguards allow us to strike this balance: the safeguards are in place, but our data is not accessible to Anthropic without our permission.

It gives us control of our data and control of the risk mitigation and the actions we decide to take after a safeguard is triggered. I think we share a responsibility to make sure these models are used safely and effectively in the world.

When your team walked us through the design, it was clear that you heard our feedback. You put us in the driver's seat. This allows us to protect our data while still being responsible stewards of the capabilities of these models.

How Enterprise Frontier Safeguards fit with the safety monitoring you already run on AI deployments Uber?

We've done a ton of work since the very beginning on how we deploy AI safely within Uber. We recently open-sourced a product called AI Detection and Response (ADR) (opens in new tab), designed to gather real-time telemetry and take real-time action in the agent harnesses we deploy.

It complements Anthropic's safeguards, because we now have access to enhanced data to detect when an agent is acting outside its bounds and respond in real time. We have our own view of what's going on, plus output from Anthropic's classifier, and we can integrate both into our overall detection environment, much like a traditional cybersecurity one. It's all about assembling context effectively to reach a decision as fast, and with as much certainty, as possible.

I think we'll see Enterprise Frontier Safeguards feed into ADR as a data source. Together with our LLM gateway, which builds a perimeter and controls how AI is used within Uber, those make up our overall AI security architecture.

Where do you think defenders should prioritize their focus next when it comes to securing AI systems?

Number one is real-time detection and intervention: getting as close as we can to the human entering a prompt in a harness, to be able to tell them, "You probably don't want to do that," or "The tool this model is about to call, the place it's about to connect to, is probably not something you want to happen."

Number two is better understanding emerging patterns. We look at trends in model behavior and detect new behaviors we didn't know were possible. That becomes a cycle. We look at the data, in many cases with the assistance of LLMs, discover these behaviors as they appear, and build safeguards against them back into the real-time platform. Then new behaviors emerge, because constraints create new behaviors, and we find those too.

What would you tell other leaders who are hesitant about the monitoring frontier models require?

AI adoption is a business imperative. It's coming whether we want it or not, and it's going to bring real benefits to businesses and people around the world. But there's also real potential for harm, and the stakes rise as models get more capable and take on more complex, autonomous work.

Every company already runs an insider threat program for its people. Nobody argues about that. We accept the sometimes onerous data retention, and we monitor things we'd rather not monitor, because we know humans occasionally act outside the bounds of their role, for any number of reasons.

Frontier models introduce the same risk. These models may be directed to act outside the constraints we expect them to operate within. So we need the equivalent capability for AI. That insider threat program for models is going to be essential to rolling these systems out safely and securely.

Learn more about Enterprise Frontier Safeguards (opens in new tab).
